articles.title: Indústria do tomate no Brasil: o papel do interior de SP em livro | G1
articles.standfirst: Obra do pesquisador Paulo César Tavares de Melo mostra que Jundiaí e municípios como Mairinque, Piedade, Presidente Prudente e Araçatuba ajudaram a moldar a história do setor no país.
articles.summary: O pesquisador Paulo César Tavares de Melo, da USP, detalha em sua nova obra como cidades paulistas moldaram a indústria do tomate no Brasil desde 1890.
articles.body:
Jundiaí (SP) teve papel decisivo na consolidação da indústria de tomate no Brasil, segundo o livro História da Agroindústria do Tomate no Brasil: do Agreste Pernambucano ao Cerrado Goiano. A obra, escrita pelo pesquisador Paulo César Tavares de Melo — mestre e doutor com mais de cinco décadas dedicadas ao estudo do tomate industrial — também destaca cidades como Mairinque , Piedade , Presidente Prudente e Araçatuba na produção do fruto.

O livro reconstrói a trajetória do setor desde o início da industrialização, em 1890, até os dias atuais, passando pelo Agreste pernambucano e chegando ao Cerrado goiano. Nesse percurso, municípios das regiões de Jundiaí e Sorocaba aparecem como protagonistas em diferentes momentos da história.

Segundo o autor, a instalação da fábrica que deu origem à Cica (Companhia Industrial de Conservas Alimentícias), em 1941, não foi acaso. Jundiaí era, naquela época, um entroncamento ferroviário estratégico, o que facilitava o escoamento da produção para o interior, o litoral e a capital paulista.

Interior de São Paulo teve papel vital no desenvolvimento da indústria do tomate no Brasil — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

A empresa nasceu da união de famílias de origem italiana, entre elas Salvador Messina, a família Rapa e o banqueiro Bonfiglioli, ligadas ao comércio de secos e molhados em São Paulo. Anos depois, outra família da região, os Pauletti, que já produzia conservas de azeitona, criou a marca Etti, que se tornaria a segunda maior indústria de tomate do país.

"Jundiaí teve um papel fundamental nesse processo de industrialização do tomate no Brasil. A fábrica começou a funcionar em 1941 porque, naquela época, a cidade era um entroncamento das principais vias férreas, tanto para o interior quanto para o litoral e para a capital", afirmou o pesquisador.

Outro capítulo da obra é dedicado à chegada dos imigrantes japoneses, a partir de 1908, aos chamados subúrbios rurais de São Paulo, com destaque para Mairinque e Cotia. Vindos inicialmente para a lavoura de café, eles migraram para a produção de hortaliças e, na sequência, para o tomate.

Foi esse grupo de produtores que, sem apoio de programas oficiais de melhoramento, selecionou na década de 1940 o tomate Santa Cruz, variedade que se tornaria referência no país. A partir daí, a produção se espalhou para Piedade, na região de Sorocaba, Indaiatuba e outros municípios do entorno de Campinas .

"Os japoneses vieram se estabelecer nos subúrbios rurais de São Paulo, principalmente na região de Mairinque e de Cotia. Com mão de obra familiar, perceberam que aquilo seria uma grande oportunidade e expandiram a produção de tomate por regiões como Piedade e Sorocaba", disse Tavares de Melo.

O livro também mapeia a virada do setor para o Noroeste Paulista, a partir do fim da década de 1970. A região de Monte Alto e Taquaritinga, até então principal polo produtor, perdeu espaço para novas áreas com terras mais baratas e clima favorável.

Foi nesse contexto que a Cica instalou uma fábrica em Presidente Prudente e a Etti ergueu em Araçatuba o que, segundo o autor, era a maior fábrica de tomate da América Latina na época. A fartura de pastagens na região permitiu a conversão de áreas para o cultivo em larga escala.

"A Etti instalou em Araçatuba a maior fábrica de tomate da América Latina daquela época. A Cica, por sua vez, instalou uma fábrica em Presidente Prudente. Ali havia terras mais baratas e farta pastagem que pôde ser convertida em campos de tomate", relatou o pesquisador.

De Monte Alto ao Cerrado: uma cultura 'nômade'

De acordo com o livro, o tomate industrial se comportou como uma cultura nômade dentro do estado de São Paulo. Conflitos recorrentes entre indústria e produtores por causa do preço da matéria-prima, somados à baixa produtividade do tomate Santa Cruz, empurraram o cultivo para novas fronteiras, culminando na virada para o Cerrado goiano no início dos anos 1980.

A diferença de produtividade entre as variedades antigas e as atuais, segundo o autor, ajuda a explicar essa migração. Em entrevista ao g1 , o professor destacou o salto tecnológico do setor nas últimas décadas.

"Naquela época se falava de 25 a 35 toneladas por hectare. Hoje, com os híbridos plantados no Cerrado, estamos falando de 100 a 120 toneladas por hectare", disse Tavares de Melo em entrevista ao g1 .

Um dos capítulos mais curiosos da obra trata do mascote Jotalhão, criado por Maurício de Sousa ainda nas décadas de 1940 e 1950 para a Cica. O personagem fez tanto sucesso que consumidores passavam a pedir "extrato elefante" nos mercados em vez de citar a marca Cica.

Após a falência do Banco Auxiliar, que financiava a Cica, a empresa passou por um grupo italiano até chegar à Unilever, que depois vendeu a operação à Cargill, hoje a maior processadora de tomate do Brasil. Junto com a fábrica, a Cargill adquiriu os direitos sobre o Jotalhão, hoje usado em linhas de extrato de tomate puro, além da marca de molhos Pomarola, também originada da Cica.

A obra também acompanha o desdobramento das famílias fundadoras da indústria de tomate de Jundiaí. Ligada à família Pauletti, a empresa Qualimax, também sediada na cidade, criou a marca Quero, posteriormente adquirida pela Heinz. A companhia americana teve, mais tarde, seu controle global ligado ao fundo 3G Capital, de investidores brasileiros, em parceria com o investidor Warren Buffett.

Já a Etti foi vendida ao grupo paulista Fenícia e, depois, à Arisco. Hoje, segundo o livro, a maior indústria genuinamente brasileira do setor é a Predilecta, de Matão (SP), que reúne marcas como Salsaretti, Estrela D'Oro e Minas Mais, esta última herdada de uma antiga unidade da Cica em Patos de Minas (MG).

Fachada da Cica em Jundiai (SP) — Foto: Maurício Ferreira / Sebo Jundiaí

O tomate hoje: do Cerrado goiano à importação

Segundo dados citados no livro, o Cerrado goiano é hoje a maior área de produção de tomate industrial da América Latina, ao sul do México, com cerca de 18 mil a 20 mil hectares cultivados por ano e produtividade média de 120 a 130 toneladas por hectare, usando 100% de sementes híbridas. A produção nacional gira em torno de 1,2 milhão a 1,3 milhão de toneladas anuais, mas o Brasil ainda precisa importar tomate para atender à demanda interna.

Relevância econômica da cultura, segundo o pesquisador:

Tomate e batata são as duas hortaliças mais importantes do PIB agrícola brasileiro

O tomate se sobressai por envolver dois mercados complementares, o de mesa e o industrial

A cultura segue como referência em geração de emprego e renda nas regiões produtoras

"O tomate, junto com a batata, é um dos itens mais importantes da produção de hortaliças dentro do PIB da agricultura brasileira. Ele acaba sendo mais relevante até do que culturas importantes como feijão e banana, porque envolve dois segmentos: o de mesa e o industrial", afirmou o pesquisador.

Livro de pesquisador da USP destaca interior de São Paulo com papel vital no desenvolvimento da indústria do tomate no Brasil — Foto: USP/Esalq/Divulgação

Autor da obra, Paulo César Tavares de Melo é mestre e doutor e soma mais de 50 anos de trabalho dedicados ao tomate industrial. Ele foi do Instituto Interamericano de Cooperação para a Agricultura (IICA), em Brasília, é docente do Departamento de Produção Vegetal da Escola Superior de Agricultura Luiz de Queiroz (Esalq), da Universidade de São Paulo (USP), e membro titular da Academia Brasileira de Ciência Agronômica (ABCA).

Sua trajetória com a cultura começou em 1972, como estagiário em uma estação experimental do Instituto de Pesquisas Agronômicas de Pernambuco. Mais tarde, cursou doutorado no Departamento de Genética da Esalq, atuou por 15 anos como geneticista e melhorista em uma empresa americana na Califórnia e foi representante brasileiro no Conselho Mundial de Tomate Industrial, com sede em Avignon, na França, o que o levou a conhecer regiões produtoras em diversos países.

"Considero o ano zero do meu trabalho com o tomate industrial em 1972, quando conheci o professor Edward Tigchelaar, da Universidade de Purdue, que testava 113 variedades de tomate industrial que entravam no Brasil pela primeira vez", contou Tavares de Melo.

Segundo o autor, o livro sobre a agroindústria do tomate surgiu como um desdobramento de um projeto maior, iniciado durante a pandemia, quando se aposentou. O material original, de cerca de 500 páginas, reuniu tantas histórias que a esposa do pesquisador, também pesquisadora do Instituto Agronômico, sugeriu que fosse dividido em duas publicações.

Os dois livros, "História das Hortaliças no Brasil, do Descobrimento aos Tempos Atuais" e "História da Agroindústria do Tomate no Brasil: do Agreste Pernambucano ao Cerrado Goiano", foram lançados no Congresso Brasileiro de Olericultura, realizado na Universidade de Brasília (UNB).

articles.title: Dentista do interior de SP conquista prêmio global por saúde inclusiva | G1
articles.standfirst: Cristhiane Olivia Ferreira do Amaral, de 56 anos, atua como cirurgiã-dentista há 34 anos em Presidente Prudente (SP), com foco nas pessoas com deficiência, síndromes, doenças raras e condições clínicas complexas.
articles.summary: A cirurgiã-dentista Cristhiane Olivia Ferreira do Amaral, de Presidente Prudente (SP), conquistou um prêmio global de saúde inclusiva após passar por um processo internacional.
articles.body:
A cirurgiã-dentista Cristhiane Olivia Ferreira do Amaral, de Presidente Prudente (SP), conquistou um prêmio global de saúde inclusiva após passar por um processo internacional rigoroso de avaliação da trajetória profissional, dedicada ao atendimento de pessoas com deficiência, síndromes e doenças raras.

Ao g1 , a profissional de 56 anos descreve a importância do prêmio Fellowship International Association for Disability and Oral Health (iADH), traduzido como “Saúde Inclusiva: Priorizando Diversidade, Equidade e Saúde Bucal”, em português.

A cerimônia ocorreu em Dublin, na Irlanda, em 22 de agosto deste ano. Segundo a pesquisadora, o candidato passa por um processo rigoroso e exaustivo de avaliação para conseguir o título.

“O Fellowship tem uma dimensão completamente diferente. Precisa documentar e comprovar diferentes dimensões de sua carreira, concorrendo ao reconhecimento com profissionais de 76 países, de todos os continentes”, relembra.

Cirurgiã-dentista há 34 anos, sendo três décadas também dedicadas à docência na Universidade do Oeste Paulista (Unoeste), Cristhiane concilia a docência, assistência e pesquisa, com uma trajetória especialmente dedicada a pessoas com deficiência, síndromes, doenças raras e condições clínicas complexas.

Cirurgiã-dentista de Presidente Prudente (SP), Cristhiane Olivia Ferreira do Amaral, de 56 anos, conquistou um prêmio global por saúde inclusiva — Foto: Cristhiane Olivia Ferreira do Amaral/Arquivo pessoal

“Durante todos esses anos, muitas vezes acordei pensando no que ainda poderia fazer por essas pessoas: o que poderia melhorar no atendimento, o que ainda precisava estudar, pesquisar ou ensinar.”

Cristhiane afirma que o reconhecimento a partir do prêmio não está ligado apenas a uma etapa da carreira. “Ele reúne aquilo que procurei construir durante décadas: o cuidado clínico às pessoas com deficiência, a pesquisa, o ensino, a atuação profissional e social e a defesa de um atendimento odontológico mais inclusivo.”

“Para mim, o Fellowship representa o ápice da minha trajetória na odontologia para pacientes com necessidades especiais.”

A avaliação do prêmio foi estruturada em cinco grandes domínios: atuação na iADH; formação e prática clínica no cuidado às pessoas com deficiência; pesquisa e produção científica; educação e ensino; e engajamento comunitário e extensão, segundo a participante.

Aproximadamente 20 profissionais foram selecionados para receber o título em 2026, sendo cinco representantes das Américas: Cristhiane e um professor de Brasília; uma profissional da Venezuela; um do México e um dos Estados Unidos.

Para concorrer ao prêmio, os participantes precisaram comprovar a trajetória profissional a partir de um extenso portfólio, passando por dois avaliadores. A aprovação da dentista de Prudente ocorreu em 30 de abril de 2026.

“Participar desse processo também me fez revisitar minha própria história. Quando reunimos documentos de tantos anos de assistência, ensino, pesquisa e atuação social, percebemos que uma trajetória é construída aos poucos, muitas vezes sem imaginar onde ela poderá chegar.”

Ela já havia recebido premiações internacionais anteriormente por trabalhos científicos apresentados em congressos no Chile, no Peru e em congressos internacionais realizados em Brasília e Natal. “Foram reconhecimentos muito importantes na minha trajetória acadêmica e científica.”

A pesquisadora acredita que o prêmio recente não representa o encerramento de uma trajetória. “Para mim, ele aumenta a responsabilidade de continuar contribuindo para a área e, principalmente, de transformar aquilo que aprendi em conhecimento que possa alcançar outras pessoas.”

Como uma de suas próximas etapas, a cirurgiã-dentista está finalizando um projeto considerado muito importante em sua trajetória, um livro que receberá o título “Odontologia para Pacientes com Síndromes, Doenças Raras e Necessidades Específicas - Diretrizes para um Atendimento Seguro e Eficaz”.

A obra, com 25 capítulos voltados ao tema, está em fase de diagramação e será lançada em breve. Ela reúne conhecimentos construídos a partir da prática clínica, da universidade, do SUS e da pesquisa.

“O livro nasceu de uma necessidade que encontrei repetidamente na clínica, na universidade, no SUS e na pesquisa: profissionais que querem oferecer um atendimento adequado, mas que precisam de conhecimento específico para tomar decisões seguras diante de síndromes, doenças raras, deficiências e condições sistêmicas complexas.”

“Se eu pudesse resumir o significado de tudo isso, diria: escolhi dedicar minha vida profissional ao cuidado de pessoas que muitas vezes encontraram barreiras para receber atendimento. E foram justamente essas pessoas que deram sentido à minha trajetória e me trouxeram até aqui”, completa.

articles.title: 'Colinha' incompleta: eleitores decidem votos na última semana | G1
articles.standfirst: Escolhas para deputado e senador costumam ficar para a reta final, enquanto escolha para presidente costuma ser definida antes. Eleições acontecem no próximo domingo, 4 de outubro.
articles.summary: O voto para deputado e senador costuma ser definido na reta final das Eleições 2026, enquanto a escolha para presidente ocorre com mais antecedência.
articles.body:
A uma semana para o primeiro turno das eleições de 2026, muitos eleitores ainda não definiram todos os candidatos em quem pretendem votar no próximo domingo (4). Enquanto parte do eleitorado já preparou a chamada “colinha” com os números dos candidatos, outros ainda avaliam opções para alguns ou todos os cargos em disputa.

O g1 ouviu eleitores em pontos da capital federal para entender por que parte das decisões fica para os últimos dias da campanha.

🔎 As eleições acontecem nos dias 4 de outubro (primeiro turno) e 25 de outubro (se houver segundo turno), das 8h às 17h (horário de Brasília). O voto é obrigatório para pessoas com idades entre 18 e 69 anos e facultativo para jovens de 16 e 17 anos e idosos com 70 anos ou mais.

A confeiteira Savina Sampaio, por exemplo, ainda não escolheu nenhum dos candidatos e diz que pretende aproveitar esta última semana para analisar os candidatos.

“[vou levar em consideração] a índole, a trajetória que veio até aqui, o que falta para eles, o que realmente querem fazer”, afirmou.

Para o cientista político Murilo Medeiros, da Universidade de Brasília (UnB), adiar algumas escolhas é um comportamento esperado diante da complexidade da eleição deste ano e, por isso, deixar essa escolha para a reta final é “natural”.

“São seis votos, centenas de candidatos, cargos muito diferentes entre si e uma quantidade enorme de informações para assimilar em poucas semanas. É natural que parte dessas escolhas fique para a reta final”, afirma.

🔎 No primeiro turno, os eleitores votam para deputado federal, deputado distrital, dois senadores, governador e presidente da República. É permitido levar uma anotação em papel com os números dos candidatos para consultar na cabine de votação.

Eleitores podem consultar "colinha" com números dos candidatos no momento da votação — Foto: Reprodução/ TRE-RS

Votos para o Legislativo costumam ficar para depois

Segundo Medeiros, os eleitores tendem a acompanhar mais de perto a disputa presidencial e deixam para os últimos dias as escolhas para cargos legislativos.

“É mais fácil identificar os concorrentes à Presidência porque a disputa recebe mais atenção. Já as escolhas para o Legislativo acabam ficando para a reta final, principalmente quando o eleitor tem menos informação sobre os candidatos”, diz.

Apesar disso, o cientista político ressalta que essas definições são fundamentais para o funcionamento do sistema político.

“O Legislativo tem papel central para definir como o país será governado nos próximos quatro anos”, afirma.

O aposentado Gilmar Mendes de Aguiar disse que, mesmo a dúvida sendo “muito pequena”, ainda não decidiu o voto para dois cargos, entre eles o de deputado federal.

Pesquisas mostram que esse comportamento é comum. Levantamento da Quaest divulgado em agosto deste ano apontou que 32% dos eleitores escolhem o candidato ao Senado na última semana antes da votação . Desse total, 14% tomam a decisão apenas no dia da eleição.

Quando o assunto é a Presidência da República, a definição costuma ocorrer mais cedo. Segundo a pesquisa, 20% dos eleitores escolhem o candidato na última semana e 10% dizem decidir apenas no dia do pleito.

O padrão também apareceu em eleições anteriores. Pesquisa Datafolha realizada após o primeiro turno de 2022 mostrou que um quarto dos eleitores decidiu os votos para o Congresso na véspera ou no dia da votação .

17% definiram o voto para o Senado no dia da eleição;

18% tomaram a decisão para a Câmara dos Deputados no próprio dia da votação.

Já para presidente, 81% dos entrevistados afirmaram ter decidido o voto pelo menos um mês antes das eleições.

O cientista político Leonardo Barreto, especialista em comportamento eleitoral, entende que as pessoas mais desinteressadas não procuram informações espontaneamente sobre deputados e senadores e esses dados “precisam chegar até essa parcela de eleitores”.

Por que deixam decisão para a última hora?

Para Barreto, a falta de interesse pela política ajuda a explicar por que parte dos eleitores adia a escolha dos candidatos.

“É aquela tarefa que você sabe que precisa fazer, mas não gostaria de fazer. Muitas pessoas não gostam de discutir política, não têm interesse e acabam deixando essa decisão para o último momento”, afirma.

Segundo Medeiros, outro motivo é a quantidade de informações que precisam ser analisadas, como propostas, trajetórias e posições.

“O custo informacional do voto é elevado. Quanto mais candidatos o eleitor precisa avaliar, mais difícil fica comparar propostas e fazer uma escolha com segurança”, explica.

A estudante de psicologia Giovanna ainda precisa decidir os votos para deputado federal e distrital. Para ela, o número de candidatos torna a escolha mais difícil.

“São muitas opções. Preciso estudar melhor as propostas para escolher quem realmente faz mais sentido para mim”, diz.

Segundo Medeiros, diferenciar as funções de um deputado federal, de um deputado distrital e de um senador também pode ser um desafio para parte dos eleitores. Para ele, conhecer essas atribuições ajuda tanto na hora de votar quanto depois, na hora de cobrar os eleitos.

A fotógrafa Ranyellen Bravo ainda não definiu três dos seis votos. Embora já tenha alguns nomes em mente, ela pretende pesquisar mais sobre os candidatos antes de concluir a “colinha”.

Para o cientista politico Leonardo Barreto, quando o eleitor não consegue chegar sozinho a uma decisão, é comum procurar alguém de confiança para ajudar a definir o voto.

“Essas decisões normalmente são tomadas em conversas com familiares e amigos, em ambientes de confiança”, afirma.

O especialista destaca, porém, que chegar à última semana sem todos os votos definidos não significa que o eleitor deixará de participar da eleição. O eleitor ainda pode buscar informações, conversar com alguém de confiança e decidir de última hora.

“A pessoa ainda pode buscar informações, conversar com alguém de confiança e tomar a decisão no último momento”, diz.

Para ele, há diferença entre indecisão e desinteresse pelo processo eleitoral.

“Quem não quer escolher e decidiu se afastar do processo eleitoral já tomou uma decisão. Isso não é mais uma indecisão”, conclui.

articles.title: Two senior FBI agents ousted over investigation into alleged harassing calls to wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller
articles.summary: Two veteran FBI agents have been removed from their jobs and reassigned over the handling of an investigation involving Katie Miller.
articles.body:
Two veteran FBI agents overseeing counterterrorism operations in the nation's capital have been removed from their jobs and reassigned over the handling of an investigation involving Katie Miller, the conservative podcaster and wife of senior White House adviser Stephen Miller, according to two people familiar with the move.

Michael Burgwald, the special agent in charge of counterterrorism matters at the FBI's Washington Field Office, and his deputy, Courtland Rae, were ousted from their positions by bureau leadership after investigators determined that allegedly harassing phone calls Katie Miller received from unknown individuals did not warrant further investigation, the sources said.

The field office team that reviewed the reported harassing calls determined they did not meet the threshold required for an FBI investigation, and no nexus to terrorism was identified, the sources said. This decision did not sit well with bureau leadership, and the two senior field office agents were removed from their positions, according to the sources.

Since taking office last year, FBI director Kash Patel — a fierce loyalist of President Donald Trump — has fired, demoted, or forced into retirement countless career employees who handled past investigations into Trump and his allies. Many of those forced out have filed lawsuits seeking reinstatement.

In a statement on an official FBI "Rapid Response" social media account established to tout the agency and respond to critics, Darren Cox, the senior executive who oversees the bureau's DC office, confirmed the ousting of Burgwald and Rae, but denied the order came from Patel.

"This was a personnel decision made at the Washington field office level alone based on our constant evaluation of mission needs," Cox said. "Any suggestion otherwise is false."

CNN is attempting to locate contact information for Burgwald and Rae. The decision to remove them from their positions has riled many rank and file FBI employees who have been critical of personnel moves they view as highly politicized, sources said.

Burgwald graduated from the United States Military Academy West Point and was the recipient of FBI investigative awards, while Rae similarly rose through the ranks of the organization after a lengthy career in national security, sources said.

The reassignment of the two senior officials was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. In a statement to Bloomberg Law, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Stephen and Katie Miller had no interaction with Burgwald or Rae, adding, "Senior leadership at the FBI determined they were stifling investigations into very serious threats and made a unilateral decision to remove them."

Still, there is a history of the Millers expressing their displeasure at the FBI's handling of personal incidents they viewed as threatening in nature. According to people familiar with an incident last year, the couple grew irate with FBI officials over pushback by career agents to use bureau resources to investigate paper flyers critical of Stephen Miller that were posted in the family's neighborhood. Like several senior Trump officials, the couple later moved into military housing.

CNN's Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
articles.summary: The foreign minister says Tehran is waiting for an official rejection of a deal, despite the US President's comments.
articles.body:
Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping within seven days because "they're losing so badly".

In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response.

He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past.

Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June.

Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.

The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.

"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers.

Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".

He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them."

Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly , told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful.

He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government".

Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?"

He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face.

Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks.

Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.

Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.

Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker.

Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage".

"President Trump's right to reject it," he said.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the US were taking a toll on Iran.

Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.

The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.

These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

articles.title: Jewish Democrats contend with another glass ceiling: Their religion
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) has emerged as one of the most closely watched contenders in the initial polling for the 2028 Democratic primary. But one factor strategists say could be a challenge for the Georgia senator is his religion. Amid party tensions over Israel and the war in Gaza, Ossoff’s rise is pushing an uncomfortable question to the…
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) has emerged as one of the most closely watched contenders in the initial polling for the 2028 Democratic primary. But one factor strategists say could be a challenge for the Georgia senator is his religion.

Amid party tensions over Israel and the war in Gaza, Ossoff’s rise is pushing an uncomfortable question to the forefront for party operatives: whether being Jewish could be another glass ceiling in presidential politics.

If Ossoff enters the race, “It’s going to be part of the conversation,” one Democratic strategist who plans to be part of the 2028 election said candidly. “Is it unfair? Yeah but it’s how our politics operate.”

It’s of particular interest among those watching the early stages of the Democratic Party’s contest given the fierce, years-long debate over U.S. support for Israel in the context of Gaza. The debate has been fierce in political primaries and led to drives for people to vote “uncommitted” when then-President Biden was running for reelection in early 2024.

While plenty of Jewish Americans and politicians are opposed to Israel’s government and its handling of Gaza, the battles have also stretched to such issues as Israel’s right to exist. Accusations of antisemitism against various politicians have also been leveled.

It also comes at a time when some Jewish voters themselves are questioning their place in the party and whether they would support candidates including Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race.

Ossoff is not the only potential 2028 contender who is Jewish. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a finalist in former Vice President Kamala Harris’s search for a running mate in 2024, is another top potential candidate. So is Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has said that his faith “influences” him.

Asked if Democratic voters would turn their backs on a Jewish candidate like Ossoff, Shapiro or Pritzker, Democratic strategist Steve Schale said, “I sure as hell hope it’s not an issue.”

“I believe, in the end, it’s going to be everything else that matters more,” added Schale, who ran former President Obama’s successful Florida operation during the 2008 presidential campaign.

Recent polling underscores why Democrats are talking about the issue.

A Politico/Public poll out earlier this year found that being of Jewish faith hurt hypothetical candidates among both Democratic and Republican voters, compared with candidates who were Christian.

A separate survey out last week found that Democrats were less likely to support candidates who regularly attended synagogue over those who only went to temple once a year or did not practice a religion. Among Republicans, however, candidates who regularly attended synagogue fared better than those who attended occasionally.

Strategists say the numbers are telling — for any of the prospective Jewish candidates.

“I think it’s going to be the big debate of ‘Do they just sort of let it lie and talk about it as it comes up or try the big head-on speech about it?’ Democratic strategist Eddie Vale said.

Vale pointed to Obama’s speech on race during his 2008 campaign and John F. Kennedy’s address on religion before he became the nation’s first Catholic president to show how candidates can turn perceptions, or even take on prejudices, head-on.

“Overcoming people’s perceptions and biases” on Judaism will be something candidates will have to overcome, Vale said. “And it’s an open question where it ends up.”

The late Sen. Joe Lieberman (Conn.) became the first Jewish candidate on a major party ticket as Al Gore’s running mate in 2000.

And when Lieberman, who was an observant Orthodox Jew, was running for president in 2004, he also found ways of discussing his religion proactively.

“He found a way to deploy faith on the campaign trail,” said Basil Smikle, the Democratic strategist who worked for Lieberman during the campaign. “I went to a Black church with [him] and he discussed his faith openly and was well-received.

“The issue isn’t religious affiliation. It’s connectivity,” Smikle added.

A candidate’s positions on Israel will come under deep scrutiny during the Democratic presidential primary no matter their religion, but it’s possible Jewish candidates will come under even more scrutiny from some voters.

Ossoff has described himself a “pro-Israel Jewish American.” He has supported aid for Israel to defend itself but has been critical of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza.

As part of that criticism, he has voted to restrict some weapons transfers to Israel, which has angered and alienated some of his Jewish constituents in Georgia.

Last month, Michael Morris, the publisher of the Atlanta Jewish Times, wrote an open letter blasting Ossoff for his Senate votes opposing Israel.

“I apologize for being blunt but please, stop lying to me and your constituents,” Morris wrote in the letter. “I hear you claim, over and over again, that you support Israel — that your support is ‘ironclad.’ It is not. You vote against Israel on the Senate floor in Washington, then come home to Georgia and make this untruthful claim.”

Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who is running against Ossoff in this year’s Senate race, has pounced on that criticism, calling the senator a “sellout” and accusing his rival of pandering to progressive Democrats while highlighting his own record of support for Israel.

While antisemitism and protests toward the Israeli government’s treatment of Gaza have increased, Smikle said, he predicted that voters will be able to look past those tensions.

Politicians, he said, “should be expected to celebrate their own faith.”

But Schale said that “religiosity in general isn’t great” among Democrats.

“I think our base has simply become very urban and secular, many of whom didn’t grow up in a family where faith was part of their lives,” he said.

He warned that as population growth shifts congressional seats and Electoral College votes toward the South after the 2030 census, it will require Democrats to “create space” in the coalition for people of faith, no matter their religion.

“If we really want to be a party that is open to all, that tent has to include people of faith, regardless of how they practice their faith,” he said.

articles.title: Supreme Court’s liberals see dash of progress on emergency appeals, or ‘shadow docket’
articles.summary: The Supreme Court’s liberal justices keep dissenting, but they also are seeing some progress on one front as the Trump administration floods the court with emergency appeals. During recent talks to judges and law students, Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson both welcomed their colleagues’ increasing willingness to pen opinions publicly explaining their fast-track…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court’s liberal justices keep dissenting, but they also are seeing some progress on one front as the Trump administration floods the court with emergency appeals.

During recent talks to judges and law students, Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson both welcomed their colleagues’ increasing willingness to pen opinions publicly explaining their fast-track decisions.

“I think it is a good and positive development,” Jackson said during a Thursday lecture at the University of the District of Columbia’s law school.

“Because now, the public and also lower courts, who are charged with responsibility of understanding what the court is doing and applying to a certain degree the court’s principles in future cases,” she continued, “really need some way to go about doing that.”

“And it was not possible before in a world in which the court was not providing any explanation.”

The Supreme Court’s emergency docket enables applicants to seek immediate relief from the justices in pending lawsuits. Many are last-ditch attempts to stave off imminent executions, but in recent years, the court has increasingly been asked to weigh in on hot-button issues.

The docket has become so controversial that court watchers can’t even agree on what to call it. Critics often dub it the “shadow docket” for the lack of explanations.

Those fast-moving cases have erupted during the second Trump administration. This week, Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed the administration’s 40th emergency application. Each represents a plea to immediately restore an aspect of the president’s agenda.

The number of emergency applications far exceeds Trump’s predecessors. During the 16 years of the Bush and Obama administrations, those two presidents only brought a combined eight emergency cases to the justices, according to research compiled by Georgetown Law professor Steve Vladeck.

After retaking the White House, Trump surpassed that count in less than four months.

To the president, the swarm of cases is the result of trial judges overstepping to block his policies. To Trump’s critics, it’s a reflection of a president acting without regard to his legal authority.

In the earlier Trump emergency cases, the high court was criticized for repeatedly siding with him without providing any public explanation.

Some of the court’s conservatives even rebutted the push. Last year, Justice Brett Kavanaugh warned the emergency cases are still in initial stages and the court should avoid a “lock-in” effect.

Kavanaugh said there’s a risk in “making a snap judgment and putting it in writing, in a written opinion that’s not going to reflect the final view.”

He was responding to criticism coming at times from lower judges, and from the Supreme Court’s liberal wing.

When Kagan last year headed to the West Coast to speak to a group of judges at an annual conference, she was asked about the emergency docket. Kagan told the crowd the most important point she wanted to make was a “need to explain things.”

“Courts are supposed to explain things. That’s what courts do,” she said, expressing her frustration with the string of recent decisions.

It was top of mind for some Democrats as they questioned Kagan during her rare appearance before Congress this summer. She defended her colleagues from some of the public criticism.

“The reason I think it’s probably not appropriate, at least not now, to call it the ‘shadow docket’ is because we have done, I think, a better job in the recent past of where appropriate — and it’s not always appropriate, but where appropriate — explaining ourselves at least to a moderate degree,” Kagan said.

The next week, Kagan was scheduled to return to the West Coast for the annual conference. Speaking to that crowd of judges once again, she confirmed her views had shifted.

“I think we have made some improvements as we’ve sort of worked our way through this,” Kagan said at the event in Bellevue, Wash., on July 23.

Sometimes, the explanations have been more lengthy.

In allowing White House ballroom construction to continue last month, the 5-4 majority explained they weren’t ruling on the project’s actual legality. Instead, they were finding the challengers likely lacked legal standing to bring the case and that Trump was likely to suffer irreparable harm if he couldn’t proceed.

Other times, the rationale has been brief. When refusing to restore Trump’s mail ballot plan , the court wrote two sentences indicating he was unlikely to succeed on the merits and the equitable factors didn’t favor him. Some court watchers called the language “cryptic.”

The explanations haven’t stopped the liberal justices from frequently dissenting when the cases go in Trump’s favor.

They did so again on Friday. Their conservative colleagues allowed the Department of Homeland Security to overhaul a key immigration tool to better police state voter rolls in advance of November’s midterm elections.

The majority’s ruling came with a seven-page explanation. Jackson’s dissent was nearly twice as long, but it’s now the latest instance that follows a new norm of both the liberals and conservatives frequently outlining their reasoning, at least to some extent.

“The Court also focuses only on the harms the Government will purportedly suffer absent a stay, disregarding the harms that the modified SAVE system has caused, and will likely continue to cause, to lawful voters,” Jackson explained in her dissent on behalf of the liberal justices.

Speaking to the law students the night before, Jackson had been asked directly about who she thinks her audience is when she’s drafting the emergency dissents. She gave no indication she was about to hand down another one.

“I am very much thinking about the American people and describing what is going on from my perspective,” she responded.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump’s media ban overshadows Xi visit as midterms clock runs down
articles.summary: The key moment of President Trump’s week did not come at the state dinner with Chinese premier Xi Jinping nor as the two leaders toured the National Archives. It came instead on social media. On Thursday afternoon, Trump proclaimed the arrival of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, as “magnificent” but bemoaned the sparsity of…
articles.body:
The key moment of President Trump’s week did not come at the state dinner with Chinese premier Xi Jinping nor as the two leaders toured the National Archives.

It came instead on social media. On Thursday afternoon, Trump proclaimed the arrival of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, as “magnificent” but bemoaned the sparsity of television coverage.

Specifically, he alleged that TV networks “didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP’” and so “they refused to be there.”

But the claim was not true. The de facto TV boycott had been sparked by a decision Trump himself made — namely, to try to ban three news outlets from the White House because he didn’t like their coverage.

Those three organizations — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — are now back after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump nominee, swiftly granted them a temporary restraining order.

Kelly’s ruling noted that the outlets are likely to succeed on the merits of their underlying case that Trump infringed upon their First Amendment rights.

It was a rare instance where a Trump attack on the media ended in a clear defeat for the president. And it added to a week that was a galling one for some Republicans, as the president blunted the impact of a major moment — the Xi visit — by his own actions.

Some might argue that Trump’s media ban created yet another distraction from his domestic difficulties. But there is a ready counterargument: An electorate that is shown, in poll after poll, to be discontent with the war in Iran, the economy and the cost of living, seems unlikely to be thrilled by a president pursuing vendettas rather than focusing on their problems.

Attacking the media and causing general uproar is something that Trump “did successfully for two decades, three decades,” said Tobe Berkovitz, a Boston University professor emeritus who specializes in political communications.

The problem, Berkovitz added, is that the main appeal of such tactics is to Trump’s most fervent fans and “even his base is shrinking. It’s not as large as it once was.”

Meanwhile, all this comes with fewer than six weeks remaining until Election Day in a midterm campaign where the GOP faces stiff headwinds.

Democrats have an 8-point advantage on the so-called genetic ballot question — when voters are asked which party they would prefer to see control Congress — according to The Hill’s data and polling partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Trump’s job performance is backed by only 39 percent of Americans in the DDHQ average, by comparison with 60 percent who disapprove.

The overwhelming consensus within the political world is that Democrats are likely to take control of the House, where Republicans currently hold a tiny majority. In the Senate, the GOP is feeling the pressure even in conservative strongholds like Texas, while Democrats who were once considered endangered — notably Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) — look increasingly safe.

The bleak picture for the GOP is leading to some modest signs of dissent inside a Republican Party over which Trump has exercised a vise-like grip for most of his second term.

GOP Senate candidates in Iowa and Michigan have recently expressed dissatisfaction with the way the war in Iran is dragging on.

Meanwhile, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), who is not up for reelection this cycle, lamented to reporters at the Capitol this past week that his party needed to do more to address voter concerns about the cost of living.

“We haven’t done a damn thing and it’s biting us in the ass right now,” the famously vivid Kennedy said.

It all adds up to a landscape where a Trump fight with the media, overshadowing the Xi visit, seems ill-advised.

To be sure, there is a different case to be made, both on Trump and Xi, and in relation to the midterms.

Trump’s loyalists could argue that the visit helped foster warmer personal relations between the two leaders. Thursday’s state dinner put major U.S. business figures, including Sam Altman, Tim Cook, Jensen Huang and Mark Zuckerberg in the same room as the Chinese leadership.

Trump himself, in another social media post Friday afternoon, insisted his meeting with the Chinese premier and his wife had been “one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the U.S.A.”

He also highlighted two meetings set for later this year — in November in China and at a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

It’s also certainly plausible that the Xi visit, even if it had gone off optimally, would have made little difference to the domestic political picture.

As for the midterms themselves, it’s possible that GOP expectations have fallen so low that even tepid results could be claimed as some kind of escape from a worst-case scenario.

More concretely, Republicans hold out hope that they could hold a top Democratic Senate target like Maine and even take some seats off the opposition party in states like Michigan, New Hampshire and perhaps even Minnesota.

But a Trump campaign schedule that next week takes him to the deep-red redoubts of Alabama and Oklahoma tells its own story.

Democrats, for their part, are perfectly content for Trump to attack the media or engage in other furors, since they believe the blizzard of controversies deepens the impression that the president is cut off from voters’ concerns.

“He has traditionally been a person who believed that all press is good press,” Democratic strategist Basil Smikle Jr. said of the president.

“But I think there are diminishing returns to that when we have reached a point of lack of attention to what voters really care about and outsize attention toward punishing people or focusing on the Kennedy Center and other physical spaces.”

Smikle added: “It just makes it look like there’s a disconnect.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Michigan man doxxed after exposing his city's booming Islamic surge takes defiant stand: 'Not gonna stop'
articles.summary: Justin Tye told Fox News Digital he won't back down after being doxxed for speaking out about mosques and Muslim immigrants in Warren, Michigan.
articles.body: A Michigan man who is facing backlash for speaking out against the growing Islamic population in his town refused to back down during an interview with Fox News Digital. "This is my home, this is where I was born and raised, this city, this state," said Justin Tye, 57, of Warren, Michigan. Tye's address was doxxed in the wake of a Fox News Digital story where he described how his town and neighborhood have been transformed by mostly Muslim immigrants over the past decade or so. He said he's received some hate mail, including a package addressed to "Justin Tye, Bigot at Large." WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH One package contained stickers reading "F— Trump and f— you for voting for him," along with a box of feminine hygiene products. But Tye isn't afraid of any backlash. "Some things are worth the trouble, and this is worth the trouble that could come from it," he said. "Being doxxed, I'm not afraid. I kind of figured this was gonna come with the territory." He also vowed to keep speaking out. BILL MAHER RIPS IMMIGRANTS WHO REFUSE TO ADAPT, SAYS AMERICAN VALUES ARE ‘NOT NEGOTIABLE’ "I'm not gonna stop. I mean, you come here from another country and you disrespect the people who have lived in this neighborhood for decades, and in many cases like myself, there's several people I went to school with that bought their parents' homes and live back here," he said, adding that he is speaking up for his neighbors too. "And that's what I've been hearing mainly is, 'finally a voice,'" he said. "These people here, these Muslims ... you need to respect the people, the Americans that are here. Stop disrespecting the people that lived here for decades." Tye said he's received encouragement from residents around town. "I'm getting a lot of support," he said. Like I was out, I had to go do some shopping. I went to Meijer, I went to the bank, and then I stopped at a pizza place to get a pizza, and all three places I was stopped by people, asked if I was the Justin that was interviewed by Fox, and I said 'yes.' And the support I'm getting is incredible." Tye and several of his neighbors spoke to Fox News Digital several weeks ago in Warren. PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH' "It all started when they bought the mosque, roughly six years ago," said Tye. "After Ramadan, they would have their [Eid al-Fitr] prayer service. It was unannounced. We didn't know anything," he continued. "All of a sudden, we were just woken up to 100-plus people behind the mosque, with an imam on a podium with big amplifier speakers, belting out his prayer service. So it woke up the whole neighborhood." TRUMP INAUGURATION PASTOR SAYS DEARBORN CHRISTIANS 'AFRAID' TO SPEAK OUT IN MUSLIM-MAJORITY CITY He described his neighborhood now as "chaos." He also took Fox News Digital on a guided tour of Warren, and pointed out five new mosques built or under construction within a seven-mile radius of his house. SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT An old industrial machinery business is now a mosque, as is a former Baptist church. Another towering mosque is under construction in the area. "Seems like every restaurant that closes up — American restaurant — there's a Muslim restaurant that opens up. I've seen four or five of them so far," one of Tye's neighbors told Fox News Digital. "I'm normally laid back. Things don't bother me," said another. "But it's like, this is my neighborhood and they're just taking it over, and that's what bothers me. And they don't care." After the initial story was published, the city released a message on social media titled, "One Warren: Stronger Together, No Room for Hate." Friday afternoon, the city responded to Tye's doxxing, and unequivocally denounced the practice. "Every Warren resident deserves to feel safe in their own community. No one should have to fear being threatened, harassed, or intimidated, simply because they chose to speak up or raise a concern." "Targeting someone at their home crosses a line," the statement said. "A person’s home should be a place of safety and privacy, never a place where they are made to feel unsafe because of their views. Regardless of where we stand on an issue, every resident deserves dignity and respect." The city noted that while not everyone will always see eye to eye, "disagreement should never become an excuse for personal attacks, intimidation, or retaliation." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There is room for everyone in Warren. There is room for disagreement, debate, protest, and advocacy. But there is no room for threats, harassment, intimidation, or hate. We should hold ourselves and one another to a standard that protects both the safety of our neighbors and the freedom to speak openly."

articles.title: SCOTUS detention fight could unleash dangerous criminal migrants onto US streets, experts warns
articles.summary: A Supreme Court battle over bond hearings for detained noncitizens with criminal records could make it harder for ICE to keep detainees locked up.
articles.body: A Supreme Court battle over whether certain noncitizens with criminal records are entitled to bond hearings during lengthy deportation proceedings could become a public safety concern by making it harder for the federal government to keep some detainees behind bars, legal experts warn. The Trump administration is asking the justices to take up Genalo v. D.C., a case involving a Dominican citizen with four criminal convictions who has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement while fighting removal. The dispute centers on a Second Circuit precedent requiring a bond hearing when mandatory immigration detention becomes "unreasonably prolonged." At that hearing, the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the detainee poses a flight risk or danger to the community. MACHETE-WIELDING MS-13 GANGSTER WANTED FOR MURDER WALKS FREE AFTER BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE RELEASES HIM: DHS Chad Mizelle, chair of litigation at the America First Policy Institute and a former acting associate attorney general and Justice Department chief of staff, told Fox News Digital the implications extend beyond immigration law. "We are talking about criminal aliens here," Mizelle said. "Those are individuals who have been accused of or convicted of an aggravated felony. Accused or convicted of murder. Accused or convicted of child rape. Accused or convicted of grievous harm upon another human being." "So these are the worst of the worst individuals," Mizelle continued. "Do we want those individuals walking the streets, re-committing, harming other individuals?" Mizelle argued Congress imposed mandatory detention on certain noncitizens with criminal records to keep them detained during removal proceedings, while the Second Circuit’s prolonged-detention rule could incentivize some detainees to drag out their cases long enough to seek bond. DOJ MOVES TO STRIP CITIZENSHIP FROM 17 PEOPLE ACCUSED OF HIDING DISTURBING CRIMES The man at the center of the administration’s latest petition, identified in court papers as D.C., is a 62-year-old Dominican citizen who illegally entered the United States and has four criminal convictions, according to court records. In 1997, D.C. was charged with multiple drug offenses, including selling and possessing a controlled substance. He failed to appear for trial, was convicted by a jury and sentenced in absentia to three to nine years in prison, but did not serve that sentence until 2024. In 2007, he was charged with possessing a forged instrument after presenting false identification to police and again failed to appear in court. In 2016, D.C. faced several charges stemming from a domestic dispute, including second-degree strangulation, third-degree assault and acting in a manner to injure a child under 17. He pleaded guilty to criminal obstruction of breathing or blood circulation and also resolved his earlier forged-instrument case with a guilty plea. Later that year, he pleaded guilty to criminal contempt. D.C. was finally arrested on the outstanding warrant from his 1998 drug conviction in April 2024. After completing his state sentence in September 2025, ICE immediately detained him while his removal proceedings continued. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT The district court subsequently ordered that D.C. receive a bond hearing under binding Second Circuit precedent but denied his separate request for immediate release. The government is now asking the Supreme Court to take the case before the Second Circuit itself rules — an unusual procedure known as certiorari before judgment. The administration turned to D.C.’s case after two other noncitizens at the center of the same legal fight saw their cases become moot. One, Carol Williams Black, had been detained for roughly seven months. His case became moot after he received a final order of removal and permanently left the United States. Black was convicted of sexually abusing a child in 2000. The Supreme Court therefore granted review in June only as to the second detainee, G.M. G.M., a lawful permanent resident from the Dominican Republic, pleaded guilty to second-degree assault in May 2015 after being accused of attacking and robbing a man during a 2012 incident in New York City. He was sentenced to two years in prison and was released early on parole in December 2016 after serving 19 months. ICE arrested G.M. at his home on Oct. 5, 2020, and detained him for 21 months without a bond hearing while removal proceedings continued. TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH The Supreme Court was scheduled to hear his case Oct. 13. But in late August, New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul granted G.M. a full and unconditional pardon for the assault conviction that had formed the basis for his deportation proceedings and mandatory detention. Solicitor General John Sauer agreed the case was moot, and the Supreme Court dismissed it Sept. 11 without ruling on the merits. The administration then identified D.C. as its replacement vehicle and asked the justices to hear the same constitutional questions this term. FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS Carrie Severino, president of Judicial Crisis Network (JCN), said the dispute is likely to affect many similar immigration cases nationwide. "This is not a question that's only going to affect D.C., the criminal Dominican national at issue in this case," Severino told Fox News Digital. "This is an issue that's going to affect criminal aliens across the country." A victory by D.C. would impose new hurdles on the government, including additional hearings and use of resources, Severino said. "As we know, immigration cases, skipping out on showing up for court dates is incredibly common," she added. "This is not something that I think the court ought to be granting on a regular basis that they'd be letting people out on bond simply on their word that they're going to be coming back when they know that they are likely to be removed." The case also raises questions about who must prove whether continued detention is necessary. The Second Circuit ruled that the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a detainee should remain in custody. "And so, if the Supreme Court winds up affirming what the Second Circuit held, that means it's going to be harder for the government to be able to detain this particular population of criminal aliens or terrorism-linked aliens," Florida State University law professor Michael Morley told Fox News Digital. "There are going to be situations where the government is not able to show that a particular person is either likely to flee or poses a risk of danger and this dangerousness by a heightened or clear and convincing standard." "It means that these criminal aliens who are already subject to removal proceedings are more likely to be released into the community while those underlying removal proceedings continue to make their way slowly through the adjudicative process," Morley continued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Supreme Court has not yet agreed to hear D.C.’s case.

articles.title: I started fact-checking Trump 10 years ago. Here are 15 things I’ve learned
articles.summary: Ten years ago this month, in my old job as Washington correspondent for the Toronto Star, I started what I believed would be a quick little side project: fac...
articles.body:
Ten years ago this month, in my old job as Washington correspondent for the Toronto Star, I started what I believed would be a quick little side project: fact-checking underdog presidential candidate Donald Trump, who was telling a remarkable number of lies but was rarely being corrected. Like a lot of people, I thought Trump would lose the 2016 election.

I was very wrong. And Trump continued to be very wrong, about a dizzying variety of subjects, for the next decade.

His relentless dishonesty has become a central feature of US and world politics. Voters and members of Congress, allies and adversaries, CEOs and investors alike have had to try to figure out how to read a man whose words are so frequently not true.

How frequently? Two months before Election Day in 2020, I had to abandon my four-year-old project of fact-checking each and every Trump statement. He was telling so many campaign lies that I'd become physically unable to look into all of them while living something loosely resembling a healthy life. By then, I'd recorded more than 8,500 false claims since September 2016.

I took a brief break from Trump-checking when he left office in 2021, replaced by a Democratic president with his own accuracy problems but nowhere near the volume or variety of Trump's falsehoods. And then, less than two years later, Trump was back at the top of the news. I counted more than 20 false or misleading claims in his 2022 speech launching his third presidential campaign. He has not gotten any more factual since.

Since I joined CNN as a fact-check reporter in 2019, I've devoted most of my reporting time to the nuts-and-bolts work of separating fact from fiction. But spending hundreds of hours immersed in Trump's rhetoric has given me some insights and personal opinions about the nature of his lying, how it is received by the public and how it is covered by the media.

Joe Biden sometimes lied, JD Vance sometimes lies, Republicans and Democrats in Congress sometimes lie, Cabinet secretaries notably including Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sometimes lie; Washington is not the nation's capital of straight shooting. But it's abundantly clear that there is no public official in Washington who lies like Trump – not as constantly, not as obviously, not about as many topics. I've heard people dismiss Trump's mendacity with a shrugging "they all lie," but we are witnessing a rare, very possibly once-in-a-lifetime political liar.

The bigger the crisis, the more Trump lies

Trump's most concerted lying sprees have come in response to political difficulties: the 2018 midterms in which his party was flailing, the 2019 Ukraine scandal that led to his first impeachment, the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic that was harming his political prospects and the 2020 election he lost . When Trump gets in trouble, he ramps up the dishonesty – even in the cases where dishonesty created some of the trouble in the first place.

The smallest lies are the most distinguishing lies

A lot of people expect politicians to try to lie their way out of a career-threatening jam or lie to make their signature policies look better. The subjects Trump has lied about include a nonexistent phone call he claimed to have received from the Boy Scouts, a nonexistent Michigan "Man of the Year" award he claimed to have received years ago, and whether there were any empty seats in venues in which seats were visibly empty . None of these things are important in the slightest, but Trump's brain has seen fit to make up a story about them. It's a special trait.

People sometimes ask how I can debunk Trump lies immediately after he utters them. I don't have any magic tricks. My (non-)secret is that he says the same untrue things again and again. The first time, it might take a while to research; by the 10th or 100th time, I can recite the debunking half-asleep – and there actually is a 100th time for some of the lies.

Like a bad poker player, Trump has tells that indicate he is likely lying. If he delivers a story featuring an unnamed person calling him "sir," it's often fiction . So are many of his stories about burly working-class men crying in his presence and a good portion of his stories involving one of his critics supposedly having come to him begging. What do these colorful but dubious tales have in common? They position him as a dominant figure to whom others – even large dudes – genuflect.

Poll numbers , inflation numbers , investment numbers , gas-price numbers , foreign policy numbers , crowd-size numbers , virtually every other kind of number – a staggering percentage of the figures Trump uses are incorrect. Even when an accurate statistic would make him look good, the businessman who used to inflate his reality show ratings and the size of his buildings tends to choose an inaccurate statistic that would make him look a little better. If "sir" is one of the best indications he is not telling the truth, so is him simply using a figure, any figure.

Trump is not only a supplier of bad information but a consumer of it

Trump has concocted hundreds of lies for his own advantage. But many of the laughable conspiracy theories he has promoted were borrowed from other people, and he often appears to truly believe them. That might be worse, not better. The most powerful person in the world, with access to endless expertise upon request, is not only a fabulist but a frequent dupe for other fabulists.

Trump is aware of some fact checks. He just doesn't care

Unless you count blocking me on Twitter in 2017, Trump has never publicly acknowledged my existence. But he has sometimes acknowledged he's aware of fact checks – while simultaneously sticking with the lies those fact checks corrected, evidently shameless about having had to be corrected.

For example, Trump has repeatedly noted that people have pointed out his claim that Biden presided over the very highest inflation in US history as incorrect. But then Trump has immediately gone on to repeat the very-highest-ever claim once more, insisting he still believes it. "Some people will correct me because they always love to correct me, even though I'm right about everything," he said , piling another lie on top of the initial one, during a December rendition of the routine.

Trump is now surrounded by people comfortable with his lies

During Trump's first term, White House aides would rarely respond to reporters' questions about his lies; after all, it's hard to defend the indefensible. But now he has surrounded himself with people willing to try. During his second term, official spokespeople regularly declare him "right" about things he is demonstrably wrong about. In a Republican ecosystem currently dominated by Trump loyalists, it's far from career-ending to shred your credibility with the mainstream media in service of the boss.

The mainstream media doesn't handle Trump's lying well enough

Pro-Trump media entities have shown embarrassingly little interest in addressing his lies. But more neutral outlets have regularly failed, too. On the last full day of Trump's first presidency in 2021, I wrote , "Too often, coverage of flagrantly dishonest Trump speeches still mentioned the dishonesty in passing or not at all. Too often, coverage still quoted the president's lies without explaining that they were wrong." More than five years later, these problems persist.

There are various reasons for that, including reflexive adherence to old habits, a Trump-driven deluge of breaking news and the diminished number of employed reporters. (CNN is one of very few outlets that has a full-time political fact-checker.) One of the key explanations, though, is one I wrote about back in 2017 : "Trump is a human version of computer hackers' denial-of-service attacks, flooding systems with more disinformation than they are designed to handle." If a politician tells one blatant lie, it's likely to get heavy coverage; if a politician tells blatant lies every week for years, it's likely that most outlets will cease viewing them as news and that the majority will be treated as background noise.

In other words, the media strategy that former Trump White House official Steve Bannon memorably described in 2018 – "flood the zone with sh*t" – has proved effective in getting lots of falsehoods into the public discourse virtually unchallenged.

A lot of people care about Trump's lying

When I give speeches about my work reporting on Trump's lies, one of the most common questions I get from the audience is some variation of, "Thank you, but it's clear that nobody cares, right?" I argue that this is false, too. It's clear that millions of Americans either don't believe debunkings from mainstream outlets or aren't interested in them, but it's also clear that millions of Americans want to know when and how the president is trying to deceive them.

Polls spanning Trump's entire career have found that somewhere around twice as many Americans do not think he is honest and trustworthy as think he is honest and trustworthy. He's won two presidential elections, of course, but it's not like he's ever convinced the entire population to stop caring about whether he is telling the truth.

Facts would matter even if only a few people were seeking them out. Fortunately, it's far more than a few.

…but a lot of people don't mind the lying, or even like it

One of my most eye-opening journalistic experiences was a 2017 reporting trip to two Trump-friendly communities in Ohio. Over and over, I heard the president's supporters say not merely that they didn't mind his lying but that they actively liked it – because it agitated the establishment they had come to despise. ("We've had so much crap in Washington for years, and now we have someone shaking 'em up really good," one man told me with delight.) I know that many Trump supporters often don't know he's lying or believe his policy stances outweigh the dishonesty. But I've also come to understand that there is a pro-dishonesty constituency within his base, at least when that dishonesty is perceived to target the "right" people.

Speaking without a filter helps political liars be viewed as honest

I observed this phenomenon with the first frequent political liar I covered, the bellicose former Toronto mayor Rob Ford. A politician who gives the impression that they authentically speak their mind is likely to be seen by many as honest even if a high proportion of their actual words are not true. Trump has always done badly in honesty polling, but his insult-heavy, damn-the-teleprompters style has also helped convince a segment of the populace that he is not only reasonably truthful but especially truthful.

Trump's most self-damaging lies are about prices

When Trump lies about a military deal with South Korea or Canada's agricultural policies or the actions of some Democrat somewhere, the average voter may not know or much care that he is wildly inaccurate. When he lies that every price is lower than when he took office, or that almost every price is falling "rapidly," even his most fervent supporters can see with their own eyes that he's trying to trick them. I suspect that his disastrous present polling on the cost of living, and generally poor approval ratings , are connected not only to inflation itself but also his decision to aggressively deny it exists.

Some of Trump's lies are so bizarre or trivial that I can't help but laugh. On the whole, though, his lies have been deeply harmful to the country. People died because of the Capitol riot prompted by his lies about the 2020 election. His lies downplaying Covid-19 almost certainly led to deaths , too. Specific people targeted by his lies, including journalists , judges and election workers , have faced threats and harassment. His lies have worsened innumerable public debates around critical policy issues. And American democracy itself is worse off for all the lying, too.
