articles.title: Iran ‘miscalculating’ by betting on midterms after 3-hour talks, Trump officials warn
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says Iran is waiting on midterm elections to cut a deal, but Marco Rubio warns Tehran misreads U.S. presidential powers.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Trump officials say Iran is miscalculating if it believes rising prices and the midterm elections will weaken President Donald Trump's hand in negotiations to end the nearly seven-month conflict. The administration is projecting confidence that mounting economic pressure will push Tehran toward a deal, even after three hours of talks this week ended without an announced breakthrough. "The president holds all of the cards here," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. Americans, meanwhile, are facing a mounting cost at home. The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.49 per gallon Friday, according to AAA, up from $3.16 a year ago. AAA said volatility in the Strait of Hormuz and high crude oil prices have driven the national average to its highest level ever recorded for this time of year. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged those costs Wednesday while arguing that allowing Iran to eventually obtain a nuclear weapon would carry a far greater price. THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES "It comes at a price and at a cost, there's no doubt about it," Rubio told reporters. "But the cost of not doing something about it is substantially higher, especially for future generations." Trump himself laid out the stakes in stark terms during his address to the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, presenting Tehran with a choice between reaching a deal that would allow Iran to rebuild or facing potentially devastating further U.S. action. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" But Trump predicted Tehran would ultimately choose a deal, arguing that Iranian leaders are waiting to see whether the November midterm elections weaken his position. "They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump said. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running." "I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran," Trump added. "It doesn't even enter my mind." A U.S. official told Fox News Digital Friday that discussions through mediators remained "positive and constructive," but said the administration was in no hurry to reach an agreement. "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush," the official said, adding that nearly 40 million barrels of oil had transited the strait over the previous 48 hours. The official predicted oil and gas prices would fall back to pre-conflict levels as the U.S. continues to maintain control of the strait. Trump said U.S. officials held a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials Tuesday as part of a renewed diplomatic push to end the conflict. But Rubio cautioned Wednesday against characterizing the talks as a "major breakthrough," saying they were largely a continuation of previous conversations. "I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation," Rubio said. Rubio also said the administration would make public any "good outcomes or things to announce jointly" stemming from its diplomatic engagements. No such announcement immediately followed the Iran meeting. Iran has since put forward a proposal of its own. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran presented U.S. mediators with a seven-day plan this week that would restore passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the end of the seven days if certain conditions are met, followed by renewed negotiations toward a broader agreement. The proposal draws from the memorandum of understanding Trump and Iran reached in June. A mediator told CBS News the latest discussions were positive but remained in their early stages. The stakes in Hormuz remain high. Commercial traffic through the critical oil chokepoint has been sharply disrupted during the conflict, although U.S. officials say the amount of oil moving through the strait is increasing. TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN "The diplomatic door is always open. The president is a deal maker," Pigott said. "But he's going to see the fundamental principle that they cannot have a nuclear weapon accomplished one way or another." Pigott pointed to growing oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the economic pressure Washington has imposed on Tehran as evidence that the balance remains in Trump's favor. "We are seeing oil move [through] the Strait of Hormuz, increasing every single day," Pigott said. "We're seeing the devastating effects on the Iranian regime from economic [actions]. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being denied to the regime through this blockade that we're seeing." Rubio offered a similar assessment Wednesday when asked about Trump's assertion that Iran may be waiting for the outcome of the midterm elections before making a deal. "I think the Iranians misread our system," Rubio said. "I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the president will no longer be able to do things against them." Rubio said Congress remains an important branch of government but argued Tehran misunderstands the limits of congressional power over sanctions and military action. "The president has extraordinary powers. Every president does," Rubio said. "He's the commander in chief, both constitutional and otherwise, to be able to carry out those functions." "So I think that the Iranians are fundamentally misreading our political system," Rubio continued. The administration is also confronting threats to energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have targeted Saudi Arabia as the conflict has expanded, adding another source of uncertainty for global energy markets. Rubio said Wednesday that the restart of a Saudi pipeline following attacks was "critical for their economy" and "critical for the global economy." He said energy infrastructure had been targeted by the Houthis as well as Shiite militias in Iraq that the U.S. says are backed by Iran. "Every time you guys ask me a question about the Middle East, it goes back to someone who's supported by Iran," Rubio said. Rubio said the U.S. would continue honoring its defense commitments to Saudi Arabia while declining to discuss what additional military options Trump could consider. We are living up to those commitments now."

articles.title: Trump boasts about economy, slams ‘fake news’ amid media battle
articles.summary: President Trump late Saturday boasted about the U.S. economy while accusing news outlets of “fake news” amid his battle over media coverage at the White House and of his administration. “We have the BEST FINANCIAL NUMBERS EVER, and the FAKE NEWS MEDIA refuses to report them!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. When asked on Saturday…
articles.body:
President Trump late Saturday boasted about the U.S. economy while accusing news outlets of “fake news” amid his battle over media coverage at the White House and of his administration.

“We have the BEST FINANCIAL NUMBERS EVER, and the FAKE NEWS MEDIA refuses to report them!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

When asked on Saturday by MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner about whether more supportive outlets should be part of the press pool, Trump said while leaving the White House that he did not, but that he wanted “real news, not fake news –– like you,” The Guardian reported.

Gardner asked if Trump wanted tougher questions, to which the president replied, “Be quiet,” while continuing to throw insults at media outlets, including CNN and MS NOW. The president has told reporters, usually reporters who are women, to stay “quiet” before.

Trump has long sparred with the press throughout his time in politics, but these attacks escalated with banning reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds earlier this month. The outlets sued the administration , and a federal judge restored their White House access last week.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered that the reporters’ access be restored “immediately” after an emergency hearing on Wednesday. The three outlets argued that Trump’s ban violated their due process and First Amendment rights.

Reporters were still barred from the executive mansion despite the judge’s ruling on Thursday. By Friday, CNN reported that its journalists were blocked from joining the press pool that traveled with Trump.

MS NOW and CNN journalists also reported Thursday that their precredentialed access was denied to the state dinner arrival at the White House during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit. The president praised the visit but claimed press coverage of the meeting was sparse.

“The event was magnificent — Actually made for Television but, because they’re Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP,’ they refused to be there,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “That’s why they have such poor Ratings.”

CBS, ABC, NBC and Fox News responded to the dispute by boycotting the press pool in solidarity with CNN, which had previously been in the rotation. Several Fox News contributors were among those who slammed the ban, with Fox News’s chief political analyst Brit Hume saying that if Trump “thinks this will lead to more favorable coverage, I think he’s dreaming.”

articles.title: Talarico leads Paxton by 5 points in Texas Senate race poll
articles.summary: A new poll shows Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico leading Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) by 5 points over a month before the November midterm elections. The Texas Public Opinion Research (TPOR) poll released Friday showed Talarico with 49 percent support from voters and Paxton with 44 percent support, with 3 percent saying…
articles.body:
A new poll shows Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico leading Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) by 5 points over a month before the November midterm elections.

The Texas Public Opinion Research (TPOR) poll released Friday showed Talarico with 49 percent support from voters and Paxton with 44 percent support, with 3 percent saying they are undecided. This new poll is the second in a monthly series of polling results released by TPOR. Last month’s poll showed Talarico’s ahead by 6 points, 48-42.

Independent voters favor Talarico by double digits, 58-26, with 5 percent who say they are undecided. Paxton holds the lead among white voters and voters 55 years and above. Talarico leads among Latino voters, Black voters, voters under 55, college-educated voters, men and women, the poll stated.

Voters also favor Talarico in terms of general approval at 21 percent. Seventeen percent say they view him as a “champion of ordinary people,” according to the poll. Fifteen percent of respondents say they support him for “his honesty, integrity and character” and 10 percent say they are looking for a new leader in the role.

Paxton’s general approval sits at 21 percent, with 23 percent preferring him due to respondents’ dislike of Talarico. The Texas Republican won support from 17 percent of respondents because of party loyalty and 14 percent for his record in office.

Talarico leads on the issue of the cost of living and improving Texans’ financial situations at 49 percent to Paxton’s 42 percent, with 6 percent undecided. The Democrat also leads on the issue of handling data centers and artificial intelligence, 45-40, with 11 percent undecided.

These results follow the Marist poll released last Thursday, showing Talarico with 50 percent support to Paxton’s 44 percent. Four percent said they were undecided. Talarico also leads in the NBC 5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll , with 46 percent of voters backing him and 43 percent supporting Paxton.

The Senate race, typically seen as an uphill battle for Democrats in the Lone Star State, shifted to a “ toss-up ” in the latest update from the Cook Political Report.

Republican groups like the Senate Leadership Fund’s Texas affiliate tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) have poured money into the race to keep it red and maintain GOP control in the Senate. President Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc. gave $5 million toward the race, according to a recent Federal Election Commission filing .

The TPOR survey was conducted Sept. 19-22 and included 1,007 respondents. The margin of error is 3.6 percentage points.

articles.title: Trump's Greenland obsession isn’t random. Here’s what’s at stake
articles.summary: Greenland's untapped rare earth minerals, oil and gas reserves could reshape U.S. energy security as Trump's Denmark deal expands military presence.
articles.body: Greenland may be covered in ice, but beneath its surface could be resources critical to the global economy — including rare earth minerals, nickel, copper, palladium, cobalt, oil and natural gas. The Arctic island’s location is just as valuable. Positioned between North America and Europe, Greenland sits along key military and shipping routes. As conflicts in Ukraine and Iran expose vulnerabilities in global energy and supply chains, the island has become increasingly important to the United States and other world powers. WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS Those factors help explain why President Donald Trump has spent years pushing for greater American control and influence in Greenland and why his administration recently reached a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland. The deal, which Trump signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, will expand the U.S. military presence on the island while keeping Greenland under Danish sovereignty. Here are three reasons Greenland has become one of the world’s most strategically important places. 1. Greenland could hold critical minerals the U.S. needs The United States is seeking to reduce its dependence on China and Russia for critical minerals used in electronics, batteries, energy infrastructure and defense technology. "We don’t want to be dependent on China for our rare earth minerals, and we don’t want to be dependent on Russia for them either," Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy Company and president of USFM Corporation, told Fox News Digital. FLOURISH CHART EMBED HERE: 30309299 Price’s USFM is exploring nickel, copper, palladium and cobalt deposits around Disko Island in western Greenland. He said the region could eventually rival Russia’s mineral-rich Norilsk district, though its potential remains unproven as drilling continues. 2. Greenland could become an energy source Greenland’s potential riches extend beyond minerals. Price’s Greenland Energy Company is pursuing permits for an exploratory oil well planned for 2027 on the island’s eastern side, where he said the geology resembles the petroleum-producing North Sea. "Our licenses are similar to the same petroleum system as the North Sea," Price said, adding that the company has sampled oil on and below the surface. TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER The project comes as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets and threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz a critical artery for the world’s oil supply. "One of the reasons that we are exploring for oil in Greenland is because of what’s going on in the Strait of Hormuz right now," Price said. Greenland’s oil and gas potential remains unproven and would require additional permits, exploration and investment. 3. Greenland occupies a critical military position Greenland’s strategic value also comes from its location between North America and Europe, near key air, sea and missile routes connecting the United States, Russia and Europe. The U.S. has maintained a military presence on the island for decades. Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, is the northernmost Defense Department installation and supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. Melting Arctic ice is opening new shipping routes and increasing interest from the United States, Russia and China. Price said the deal could also boost investor confidence in long-term oil, gas and mineral projects. "What it does is it shores up long-term investment in Greenland, and that’s what our projects are," Price said. "They’re long-term investments from oil, gas and minerals."

articles.title: America needs an ironclad, bipartisan commitment to press freedom
articles.summary: Donald Trump’s long-running conflict with the American news media has reached a point that demands a broader response.
articles.body:
President Trump’s long-running conflict with the American news media has reached a point that demands a broader response. I’d like to offer a proposal.

The immediate crisis is the White House’s exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on charges of peddling “ fake news ,” and the remarkable decision by ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News to refuse to replace CNN in the presidential television pool.

A federal judge has now ordered the administration to restore the three organizations’ credentials temporarily, finding they were revoked without adequate due process. Yet reporters were still being denied entry the next day, prompting another emergency appeal to the court.

By Friday, the presidential television pool was back in place and the legal wrangle was largely resolved. But the larger issue was not. Conflicts involving press credentials, government terminology, Pentagon reporting rules and federal leverage over media companies have repeatedly raised the same question: How much influence should a president have over the institutions responsible for independently covering him?

The answer now has to come from more than courts and news organizations themselves. Political leaders should be asked to put their names behind a short, bipartisan statement of principles on presidential press freedom, circulated to every member of Congress, governor, current Cabinet member and living former Cabinet member.

Such a statement would provide a simple test that survives the politics of the moment. A Republican can believe CNN treats Trump unfairly and still believe a president should have no power to punish CNN for its journalism. A Democrat can despise Fox News and still recognize that a future Democratic president should have no power to exclude Fox. Press freedom is durable only when its defenders extend it to journalism they dislike.

The television networks have provided an example. CNN was scheduled to provide pool coverage when the White House barred it. ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox could have accepted CNN’s slot. Instead, they declined, transforming another Trump-CNN confrontation into a dispute over the institutional independence of the television press.

There is instructive symmetry in Fox’s participation. In 2009, the Obama administration reportedly attempted to exclude Fox News from a pool interview with a Treasury official. Other networks objected and the administration relented. Seventeen years later, Fox is standing alongside those competitors when a Republican administration excludes CNN. The politics reversed; the institutional interest did not.

That solidarity also creates a dilemma. The president requires continuous independent coverage. The entire press corps cannot crowd into the Oval Office, board Air Force One or accompany a motorcade, so a handful of journalists witness events on everyone else’s behalf.

A prolonged suspension of that system carries its own danger. The White House increasingly becomes the source of the pictures and sound through which Americans experience their president. The press must defend its independence without surrendering its role as an independent witness.

News organizations can continue covering Trump wherever access remains available, expand sharing of video and reporting and create a consortium involving networks, wire services, newspapers and digital outlets. When official White House footage becomes necessary, broadcasters can identify it as government-produced material.

Fox and Newsmax joining would make such an approach more powerful without requiring them to endorse CNN’s journalism. They need only maintain that news organizations share an institutional interest in keeping decisions about journalism outside presidential control.

The warning signs have accumulated for years: Trump’s “ fake news ” obsession, the Associated Press access dispute over “Gulf of America,” new Pentagon restrictions on reporters and battles with media companies facing federal decisions .

Seen separately, these episodes can look idiosyncratic, even absurd. Seen together, they raise a serious concern about using government power to shape who can cover the government and on what terms.

That is why the response should extend beyond journalism. The proposed statement should be narrow enough to attract people who disagree about almost everything else. Its purpose would be to establish a rule for presidential power, not adjudicate the merits of CNN, Fox, Trump or or any particular story.

Its central principle could be simple: Regardless of which party controls the White House, the president should respect the independence of established news organizations and the press arrangements through which they cover the presidency. Officials who believe reporting is inaccurate should answer through facts and argument. Ordinary press access should operate according to consistent standards, not presidential approval or disapproval of editorial decisions.

Republican signatures would carry particular significance now, just as Democratic signatures would under a future Democratic administration confronting conservative media. The statement’s strength would come from assembling a visible group across parties and administrations willing to endorse the same institutional rule.

It should be difficult for any public official to explain why a president of either party should be able to penalize established news organizations because he dislikes their coverage.

Trump will eventually leave office, and the presidency will pass to someone else. The precedents surrounding presidential power will pass with it. Whatever comes from last week’s court fight, the principle should survive it. Presidential power over the press is not ultimately about the media. It is about those the media serves: the people.

Dan Perry is the former London-based Europe-Africa editor and Cairo-based Middle East editor for the Associated Press, the former chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and the author of two books.

Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) on Sunday predicted that Democrats will impeach President Trump for a third time between his two presidencies if they take control of the House after the November midterm elections.

Jordan suggested in an interview on “ Cats Roundtable ,” the WABC 770 AM radio show hosted by John Catsimatidis, that Democrats will take the legislative branch’s oversight capability “and turn it into a weaponization of government.”

“They say they’re not going to, but we know they will –– they’ll do a third impeachment of President Trump,” Jordan told the host. “But that’s just part of it. They’re going to investigate the first family, they’re going to investigate cabinet secretaries.”

Jordan said Democrats, specifically naming the senior Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), will also look to impeach FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should they win back the House.

“And then they’ll also, I think, go after people in the private sector,” Jordan continued. “They’re going to go up for any business who, as an example, you got businesses who helped paper the inauguration, which happened every four years … [Democrats] are going to somehow say, ‘Oh, these businesses have done something wrong.'”

The Ohio Republican also speculated that Democrats could attempt to go after the 2028 Republican nominee for president and their running mate, calling it “nonstop weaponized investigations.”

“Not for legitimate oversight, but to just go after your political opponents,” Jordan added.

Decision Desk HQ’s forecast shows a 72 percent probability that Democrats will win back the House.

It’s unclear if Democrats will go forward with another Trump impeachment after the previous two during and shortly after the end of his first term concluded with acquittals .

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said he has not ruled out pursuing another impeachment of the president, though he added that Raskin and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform will lead the charge to hold the president accountable if they become chairs of their respective committees.

Trump himself has warned Republicans that they must keep control of the House or he could face another impeachment. He said it again last month at a rally for South Carolina Republican Sen. Darline Graham, adding that Democrats seeking to impeach him “have no idea why.”

An earlier attempt to impeach Trump over his deportation agenda, spearheaded by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas), failed this month . Green accused the president of abusing his powers by launching an immigration crackdown, resulting in the deaths of U.S. citizens.

The House first impeached Trump in 2019 over his threat to withhold military aid to Ukraine if its president, Volodymyr Zelensky, did not investigate then-presidential candidate Joe Biden. Trump was impeached again following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. He was already out of office when the Senate voted to acquit him.

articles.title: Blanche addresses White House press ban, calls access 'a privilege ... not a right'
articles.summary: The attorney general disputed that the president "denied access" to outlets.
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday addressed the Trump administration's decision to ban three mainstream news outlets from accessing the White House, saying that President Donald Trump had not "denied access" to the organizations and asserting that it is a "privilege ... not a right" to be at the White House.

"The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it. This is -- what the president has said is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news," Blanche said in an exclusive interview with "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz. "There's still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing, Martha, is to know that ... being in the White House is a privilege. It's not a right."

In the early hours Thursday, Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that required the White House to temporarily restore credentials of journalists working for CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Kelly said in his ruling that he believed the outlets cleared the "high bar" required to grant a TRO.

Journalists were allowed back onto the White House grounds later Thursday and primary television pool coverage resumed Friday for the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's official state visit. But on Saturday, there was no TV pool coverage for the president's trip to a football game in Tennessee; CNN was scheduled to be network covering the president that day, but they said their access to Air Force One was blocked.

Blanche said it wasn't unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed onto the president's plane.

"The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One. This wasn't a a one-time denial of CNN. There's all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying," according to Blanche, who added, "it's not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it's common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president."

Blanche claimed the three news outlets that were subject to the White House ban "refuse to report anything accurately," which he said presented a "national security problem."

"When you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House that affects our relationship with our foreign partners, that affects our relationship with our foreign enemies -- and so this is just not about the fact that they're refusing to report accurate news. It's all about the information that the American people have a right to hear coming out of of our what should be respected media outlets."

Judge Kelly, however, was skeptical in his TRO ruling that national security was the true reason for the ban.

"For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House -- instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs' reporting," Kelly wrote.

Hours after announcing the ban on social media, Trump was asked in the Oval Office if there was any "particular reason or particular story" that prompted it.

"No, no. It's -- it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it," the president said.

On "This Week," Blanche said he wouldn't "get into what the judge says" because the litigation is ongoing, but added "our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security."

When Raddatz pressed Blanche to provide specific examples of stories with which the White House has taken issue, Blanche declined to do so.

Artificial intelligence 'vital to our national security'

On the issue of artificial intelligence, the attorney general echoed the president's position on the technology, describing it as "so important and vital to our national security interests and to the success of this country that the United States lead in this space."

Trump has said it's critical that the U.S. continues to dominate the AI space, citing competition with China specifically.

"Whoever wins AI, WINS! We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I'm going to keep it that way! I'm not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself," he posted on social media Monday.

Some AI company leaders are calling for an industry-wide slowdown amid growing concerns about how the rapid pace of development. Multiple incidents of AI agents acting autonomously have come to light in recent months, including instances where AI agents infiltrated outside companies without the agents' parent companies' awareness as it happened.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that OpenAI agent "infiltrated" a government public health website earlier this summer. This weekend, OpenAI confirmed that its models interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, behavior the company discovered amid an ongoing review into its AI agents' behaviors.

Blanche acknowledged that "there's going to be adjustments that have to be made" around AI as the industry continues to develop, but he argued the companies themselves already have the ability to "adjust the technology" as needed.

"In the meantime, the answer is not to just try to all of a sudden try to regulate this in a way that will make us second or third place in the world as far as being being the leaders in this space," Blanche said.

During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, Trump said of AI, "We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice."

Asked what that meant, Blanche said, "What it means is that we have a ton of laws -- criminal laws, civil laws -- that are already in place and on the books that allow us to charge individuals, to charge companies in the right circumstances when there's crimes committed, and so the answer isn't always more laws, more laws, more laws."

"When there are crimes committed, we have a lot of tools already, and the federal Title 18 gives us a lot of a lot of ways to go after criminals and bad actors in the AI space and other spaces," Blanche continued. "So when the president talks about about the fact that the Department of Justice and the FBI and [Homeland Security Investigations], they can go and arrest bad actors in this space, that's what he means, and it's true, and that's what we're doing."

articles.title: The vital vaccine shield America cannot afford to lose
articles.summary: Since 1989, the U.S. government has run a program that has distributed more than $5.5 billion to individuals who have suffered adverse consequences from vaccines. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. wants to destroy it.
articles.body:
Since 1989, the U.S. government has run a program that has distributed more than $5.5 billion to individuals who have suffered adverse consequences from vaccines. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. wants to destroy it.

The National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program was signed into law by President Ronald Reagan in 1986. Congress designed this “no-fault” federal system to do two crucial things: ensure that individuals who experience exceedingly rare, severe reactions to vaccines are compensated quickly and fairly without having to slog through the federal district courts, and protect the stability of the nation’s vaccine supply.

It gives families an avenue for relief without requiring them to prove negligence by a manufacturer. Simultaneously, it protects pharmaceutical companies from catastrophic, unpredictable liability that could force them to stop making life-saving shots altogether.

The impetus was a wave of lawsuits that threatened to drive vaccine manufacturers out of business entirely. Diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccine shortages surged, prices skyrocketed, and the nation faced the terrifying prospect of losing access to basic immunizations against deadly diseases. The National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program ended those threats and allowed vaccine manufactures to continue their research and production of vaccines that have saved millions of lives since.

The program works in part by presuming causation for a specific list of injuries for each listed vaccine, relieving families from proving both negligence and causation. That list of presumed injuries has been established through a committee of experts conducting extensive scientific reviews to arrive at an agreed upon set of causation.

But Kennedy, the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, has referred to the fund not as a safety net but as a corporate shield that protects “Big Pharma” from accountability. By stripping vaccine manufacturers of their liability protections , he wants to throw vaccine injury claims back into traditional civil courts and to open the issues of negligence and causation to conventional civil litigation.

The secretary is also pursuing an additional tool, one that will eventually destroy the program while enshrining one of his central conspiracy theories in the law: He wants autism to be listed as one of the presumed causations of vaccines . Listing autism as an injury that is “presumed” to have been caused by vaccines seems likely to flood the system with claims that will ultimately drain the funds and collapse the whole enterprise.

For years, Kennedy has been promoting thoroughly debunked conspiracy theories about vaccine safety, repeatedly claiming a link between childhood immunizations and autism — a narrative rejected by every major global scientific body. But now, as the head of Health and Human Services, changes to the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program could finally give him the opportunity to give legal weight to his autism conspiracy theory.

Dismantling or undermining the compensation program today would likely trigger the same crisis the nation faced in 1989 but on a much larger scale. If manufacturers are forced to price the risk of endless, unpredictable litigation into every vial, or the consequences of listing autism as a presumed “caused” injury, vaccine prices will soar. Many companies will simply stop producing them altogether.

The result will not be safer vaccines; it will be severe shortages, preventable disease outbreaks, and a devastating blow to herd immunity that puts our most vulnerable citizens — newborns, the elderly and the immunocompromised — at grave risk.

Furthermore, dismantling the fund fundamentally harms the very families Kennedy claims to champion. Far from a hollow corporate shield, the fund has quietly and officially delivered billions of dollars in total financial compensation to more than 12,500 injured Americans since its inception.

Stripping this streamlined safety net away doesn’t protect the public; it forces families into an understaffed civil tort system where decades of grueling legal battles, astronomical attorney fees, and the nearly impossible burden of proving a manufacturer’s specific fault in a traditional court of law awaits them. The current system is not perfect — it suffers from administrative backlogs that need fixing — but replacing it with a broken litigation lottery is a disservice to victims.

Richard Sauber is a lawyer in private practice in Washington. He served as special counsel to former President Biden.

articles.title: Tillis says Trump endorsing Paxton over Cornyn was ‘colossal mistake’
articles.summary: GOP Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) on Sunday blasted President Trump for endorsing Ken Paxton (R) over Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in the Texas Senate Republican primary earlier this year. “In the case of Cornyn, he made a colossal mistake,” Tillis told host Jake Tapper on CNN’s “State of the Union.” The North Carolina Republican added,…
articles.body:
GOP Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) on Sunday blasted President Trump for endorsing Ken Paxton (R) over Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in the Texas Senate Republican primary earlier this year.

“In the case of Cornyn, he made a colossal mistake,” Tillis told host Jake Tapper on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

The North Carolina Republican added, “John Cornyn’s a great member of the U.S. Senate. Paxton has his challenges. We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in Texas if Cornyn had won.”

Trump backed Paxton over Cornyn in May, days before the Texas attorney general defeated the four-term senator and secured the right to take on Democrat James Talarico in the general election.

Talarico’s fundraising prowess has given his campaign a significant financial edge over Paxton’s, as the Democrat had more than $21.5 million on hand relative to less than $1.8 million for the Republican nominee as of the end of June, according to data from the Federal Election Commission.

The GOP-linked Senate Leadership Fund has poured millions into the race to boost Paxton, while Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC has funneled $15 million to the Lone Star State.

Tillis noted the president’s investment in the race, calling his backing of Paxton over Cornyn an “unforced error” that puts the seat in jeopardy. The Hill’s polling partner, Decision Desk HQ , gives Talarico a 56 percent chance to beat Paxton in November.

In endorsing Paxton over Cornyn, who said during the 2024 presidential campaign that the GOP should move on from Trump, the president touted the Texas attorney general’s track record as a stalwart MAGA advocate.

But the retiring Tillis noted Cornyn was also a firm backer of Trump’s agenda, saying “now is not a time for these loyalty oaths.”

He told Tapper, “Republicans that go after other Republicans for only being in the 95th percentile, I’d like for them to go find another party, because that’s unsustainable for me, as a lifelong member of the Republican Party, to live up to those expectations.”

articles.title: Cook Political Report founder: House is a ‘done deal’ for Democrats, reclaiming Senate ‘very realistic’
articles.summary: Cook Political Report founder Charlie Cook on Sunday said that it has been a “done deal” conclusion that Democrats are likely to retake the House after the November midterm elections, while their chances of claiming the Senate look “very realistic.” “I would completely agree that the House has been kind of a done deal for…
articles.body:
Cook Political Report founder Charlie Cook on Sunday said that it has been a “done deal” conclusion that Democrats are likely to retake the House after the November midterm elections, while their chances of claiming the Senate look “very realistic.”

“I would completely agree that the House has been kind of a done deal for a good while,” Cook said in an interview on ABC News’s “This Week” with Martha Raddatz. “But the Senate, a year ago, it wasn’t realistic to think that the Senate might flip, but now it’s very realistic.”

“I mean, the thing is, this is normal. It’s happened to every party in midterm elections where your people get disillusioned and turn out at low levels,” Cook said. “The other side is energized, turning out big numbers and then those fickle independent voters in the middle start breaking against you.”

He added that he expects Democrats to pick up around 20 seats in the House and four or five in the Senate. Cook said he sees this outcome in Senate with races in Michigan, North Carolina, Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire, Minnesota and “maybe” Kansas.

“But in Michigan, it’s where the focus is on President Trump,” Cook said, referring to the Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). “Boy, it’s really hurting. But when you have a Democrat nominee that’s somewhat polarizing, controversial, like you have in Michigan, that takes the attention away from Trump and goes on the Democrat.”

Cook said the race is not likely to be a “blue wave” but a “red undertow,” saying that a wave would appear more “uniform” and that “pulling down” Republicans has hit “some places more than other places.”

The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecasted a 72 percent probability that Democrats retake the House and a 54 percent possibility of winning back the Senate after November.

Polling experts have said that forecasts favoring Democratic victories in both chambers are reflected in President Trump’s tanking approval ratings, Democratic enthusiasm in the primaries and GOP candidates publicly breaking with the president over the Iran war’s effect on soaring prices.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll shows the president’s approval rating sunk to an all-time low, at 32 percent. Among Republicans, 72 percent said they approved of his performance, down from 82 percent the week before. GOP approval sat at 91 percent right after his second inauguration.

Republican support for the Iran war has also been on the decline , with some like Rogers calling for the conflict “ to end, and end quickly ,” as gas prices have soared since the conflict began in February.

articles.title: This week on The Hill: Senate packs final week before October recess
articles.summary: The Senate is heading into its final week before lawmakers leave Washington for a month-long recess, and Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is looking to make the most of the upper chamber’s remaining days. One of the biggest items on the agenda is a final vote on the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act. The legislation,…
articles.body:
The Senate is heading into its final week before lawmakers leave Washington for a month-long recess, and Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is looking to make the most of the upper chamber’s remaining days.

One of the biggest items on the agenda is a final vote on the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act. The legislation, led by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), would create federal rules for compensating college athletes, limit transfers and midseason coaching moves and set a five-year window for athletic eligibility, among other regulations.

Senators are also eyeing action on the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would mitigate the impact of data centers on Americans’ electric bills. GOP senators are targeting a procedural vote on the bill this week, but it is unclear whether Democrats will be on board — as some have argued it doesn’t go far enough in addressing the issue.

Anything Thune is unable to get across the finish line this week will likely be pushed until after the midterms, as lawmakers return to Washington into the lame-duck period.

The recess could leave GOP senators with a tight timeline in November, as they’d have less than two months to advance their priorities if Democrats potentially flip one or both chambers.

Senate to hold final vote on college sports bill: The Protect College Sports Act is expected to garner broad bipartisan support on the Senate floor.

Republicans eyeing initial vote on Ratepayer Protection Act: The bill is aimed at shielding Americans from increased electricity costs spurred by data centers.

Johnson and Trump to meet with AI executives: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and President Trump will meet with artificial intelligence industry leaders this Tuesday.

Senate holds final vote on college sports bill

The Senate will hold a final vote on the Protect College Sports Act Monday.

The legislation would protect the NCAA — the college athletics governing body — from antitrust lawsuits, establish caps on revenue sharing and allow schools to have retention funds for star players.

It also requires agents to register with a state before representing student-athletes and caps their fees at 5 percent. It also guarantees scholarships for 10 years after eligibility — so athletes can complete their degrees after their playing days — and requires Division I schools to provide medical coverage for them.

The legislation, however, has previously received pushback from the NAACP and the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC), as well as the AFL-CIO and its sports council.

The CBC wrote in a letter to Cruz and Cantwell, the top Republican and Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, that “for generations, Black athletes have helped build college athletics into one of the most powerful and profitable industries in American life.”

“(The caucus) believes institutions that profit from Black talent and Black communities have a responsibility to stand with those communities when their fundamental rights are under attack,” the group wrote. “Silence in the face of injustice is not neutrality—it is complicity.”

Cruz defended the act in remarks last week, saying, “In getting the bill to the Senate floor, we enhanced NCAA oversight and accountability, gave states the ability to impose stronger health and safety protections, protected existing broadcast contracts, and softened conference realignment restrictions in certain cases.”

“Not everyone got everything they wanted. Frankly, I didn’t. And neither did my counterpart, Ranking Member Maria Cantwell. But this is what legislating means. It means Republicans and Democrats listening to each other and finding middle ground. It means compromising to reach an agreement. It is the way our founding fathers designed the legislative process for the good of the whole,” he added.

Senate to hold procedural vote on data center bill

Senate Republicans are eyeing an initial vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act this Wednesday, according to Politico .

The bill, championed by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), requires states to consider adopting standards that would force tech companies to shoulder the electricity cost increases associated with large data centers — but it doesn’t actually require states to regulate them.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) had previously blocked Husted’s effort to unanimously pass the bill earlier this month. Critics, including the New Mexico Democrat, have argued that the legislation is toothless and may not spur significant changes at a time when AI data centers threaten to drive up electricity costs and destabilize the grid.

But Husted said on the 10-Minute Drill podcast, “The president wants it. House Democrats and Republicans want it. Consumers want it. The business community wants it.”

“They just had to not object to it, and it would be on the president’s desk. It would have already been signed, and we would have a law in the land that requires states to force data centers to pay their own way when it comes to electricity. But the Democrats blocked it, so I’m not going to give up on it,” Husted continued.

It’s not clear how much support the bill will have from Senate Democrats.

Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), told Politico that the bill “is an effort to rescue Husted’s campaign.” Husted is up for reelection in a competitive seat that is rated as a toss-up by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

Johnson, Trump to meet with AI executives

Johnson and Trump are scheduled to meet with AI executives this Tuesday, according to NewsNation.

The meeting comes as a trio of Big Tech trailblazers — Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk, of Tesla and SpaceX — stepped forward to urge a deceleration in the development of AI, citing the risks of global catastrophe.

Amodei penned a long blog post warning that a failure to tap the brakes on the emerging technology — urging developers to focus more intently on the safety risks associated with unleashing AI systems capable of orchestrating bioterrorist attacks, economic upheaval and other cataclysms.

While House Democrats and some Republicans have urged Congress to quickly pass bills that would address the issue, Johnson has previously said that he wants a “balanced approach” when it comes to implementing guardrails.

“The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and in hyperregulation. If you do that, then you lose your edge, and that is a national security concern for the American people,” Johnson said.

Rachel Frazin and Alexander Bolton contributed to this report.

articles.title: GOP fears ‘perfect storm’ could lead to Marshall’s loss in red state Kansas
articles.summary: It’s been nearly a century since Kansas voters sent a Democrat to the Senate. But Adam Hamilton, a prominent pastor, is looking to make that jump as Republicans grow more and more unsettled about incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall’s chances in the heartland. “It’s all or nothing in a sense, because the story is that…
articles.body:
It’s been nearly a century since Kansas voters sent a Democrat to the Senate.

But Adam Hamilton, a prominent pastor, is looking to make that jump as Republicans grow more and more unsettled about incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall’s chances in the heartland.

“It’s all or nothing in a sense, because the story is that after 96 years, a Democrat could win a Senate seat in Kansas, but it also could be that there’s a reason for it not happening in 96 years, that Marshall pulls it out simply because it’s so difficult,” said Bob Beatty, professor of political science at Washburn University in Topeka.

Elections analysts have moved the Kansas Senate race to the left in recent weeks as polls indicate that, like elsewhere around the country, President Trump’s low approval rating is dragging down Republican candidates. Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia both shifted the race to “Lean Republican” from “Likely Republican” last week.

Kansas is generally a red state, although it has sometimes elected moderate Democratic governors. Trump won Kansas in 2024 by 16 points. But his approval rating in the state now hovers around 40 percent, while Hamilton polls slightly ahead of Marshall at 45 percent to 43 percent, according to a recent Emerson College/Nexstar poll . That mirrors many other red states — like nearby Iowa — where Republican candidates are facing negative public opinion about tariffs, the war in Iran and the resulting high prices.

Beatty said Hamilton is a uniquely strong Democratic contender to capitalize on that national trend. Hamilton has never held political office but has been the pastor of a network of United Methodist churches he founded in the Kansas City metro area for 36 years.

Marshall’s Republican primary opponent Arch Naramore, who won more than 20 percent of the vote, endorsed Hamilton on Thursday.

The Marshall campaign and national Republicans have seized on Hamilton’s faith in their messaging against him — calling him a “megachurch pastor” and pulling quotes from his sermons to depict him as “woke” on gender and sexuality, climate change and Black Lives Matter.

“I just don’t know if it’s a bad thing in Kansas to be a pastor of a megachurch,” said Beatty. “But that’s how they’re going after him right now.”

Vice President Vance, on a campaign stop for Marshall in Olathe earlier this month, condemned Hamilton’s church for hosting a Pride festival and brought up quotes from Hamilton’s sermons seeming to indicate Hamilton has condemned eating meat and “white privilege.” It’s reminiscent of Republicans’ attacks on the Democratic candidate, Texas state Rep. James Talarico, in the Lone Star State’s Senate race.

“In this race, we have got Dr. Roger Marshall, a proud servant of this state, and a proud Christian to boot, versus a guy who would insult your faith and spit on your religion to accrue donations to himself,” Vance said.

Hamilton has also made waves since emerging from a crowded primary field in August by hitting the airwaves with measured oratory and polished digital media from his training as a pastor and evangelist. Although he entered the race late, he raised $1 million within the first week of the campaign in May, and his fundraising has only soared since then.

Both the Marshall and Hamilton campaigns declined to comment on the record about the dynamics of the race.

Marshall, a former obstetrician finishing his first term in the Senate, has generally been a defender of Trump’s agenda. He goes by “Doc” around the Senate and on the campaign trail, and has leaned into his career while championing the Trump administration’s health initiatives — including starting a “Make America Healthy Again” caucus before Trump even took office.

But the Trump platform isn’t as strong as a message on the campaign trail anymore. In recent weeks, Marshall has had to push back on Trump administration moves that don’t go over well in Kansas. When Trump mused about banning sales of Bombardier — a Canadian private jet maker with a large workforce in Kansas — amid his trade war with the U.S.’s northern neighbor, Marshall spoke out.

“I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Marshall posted on social media.

And last week, after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents suddenly swept through southern Kansas , ensnaring the agricultural and meatpacking workforce, Marshall also took to social media to urge federal agencies to work more closely with local police.

“When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement. Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone, and working together keeps officers and residents safe,” Marshall wrote.

Meanwhile, Hamilton and national Democrats are looking to hit Marshall over his ties to Trump and the war. They’re also hoping to benefit from a New York Times investigation that alleged Marshall had sued multiple patients for medical debt while working as a doctor. The Hamilton campaign released an ad Friday morning starring one such patient, who said she had been arrested over the charge.

The “perfect storm” of Hamilton’s profile, Trump’s unpopularity and Marshall’s history might be just enough to overcome the high odds for Democrats in Kansas, Beatty said.

“If there’s any kind of national blue wave, whether it’s a small one or a big one, I think then Hamilton has got a really good chance, and it’s just hard to even say that because I’m from Kansas,” Beatty said.

“I think he can win on his own. It would be tough. But you put in a little wave there, or a big wave, it’s very, very possible.”

images.caption: Adam Hamilton, a Methodist mega-church pastor from Kansas, talks to voters as he wraps up a U.S. Senate listening tour on April 18, 2026, at Limitless Brewing in Lenexa, Kansas.

articles.title: To mitigate Himalayan disasters, Beijing must abandon its narrow, fear-based controls
articles.summary: Following a devastating flood on Aug. 26, critics accused Beijing of suppressing casualty figures and blamed regional instability on aggressive hydroelectric dam construction in the fragile Himalayan ecosystem.
articles.body:
The latest death toll of the Tibet-Nepal flood on Aug. 26 is now reported to be 1,453, with 5,200 still missing. But this reflects exclusively on the Nepali side. Under Chinese control, the Tibetan people are deprived not only of basic human rights in life, but the right to have their deaths openly recognized is denied by Beijing’s impulse to restrict information.

On the day the flood struck, the Kyirong County administration in Tibet launched a WeChat alert system for residents to report missing family members. But after the registered missing reached 219 people, the authorities suddenly shut the system down, according to a reliable source in Kathmandu. Social media posts are blocked and citizens who contradict official death tolls, which stands at just 43, face fines of up to $150 or ten days in detention.

Critics contend that these information controls are designed to shield the root causes of such disasters from scrutiny.

Himalayan communities and civil societies have called for an immediate halt to mega-dam construction.

Critics and Chinese researchers alike have long tied regional disasters to Beijing’s aggressive dam -building across Tibetan rivers. But China continues to expand onto the Himalayas’ southern slopes, funding over a quarter of Nepal’s 570 hydropower projects.

This expansion is a clear geopolitical strategy. By financing Nepal’s power plants and supplying Chinese electric vehicles, Beijing aims to break Nepal’s traditional energy reliance on Indian oil and gas.

However, building massive reservoirs beneath fragile Himalayan glaciers where temperatures are already rising twice as fast as the global average, creates a serious environmental threat. Reservoirs pool immense volumes of surface water under the intense high-altitude sun and act as giant heat sinks which creates a localized greenhouse loop in the glacial zone. While scientists widely report this effect in expanding natural glacial lakes , man-made dam reservoirs built in the valleys directly beneath Himalayan glaciers produce the exact same warming dynamic. Therefore, for people in the Himalayas, the dams represent an existential risk that must not be ignored.

For decades, scientists have warned of the danger of Himalayan glacial lakes bursting as a result of global warming. Today, villages and towns in Tibet, Nepal, India, and Bhutan live under a nuclear weapon-like ticking threat hanging directly above them. There are at least 14,000 lakes trapped across the world’s highest mountain range. Now, as temperatures in the Himalayas surge, glacial melting is accelerating, giving rise to larger, deeper, and more lethal lakes.

A 9th-century treaty between Tibet and China declared: “Tibetans shall be happy in Tibet, and Chinese shall be happy in China.” This principle echoes the traditional Chinese proverb: “Those living near mountains live off the mountains; those living near water live off the water.” The Chinese civilization developed in the lowland river basins of East Asia, and Tibetan civilization thrived high on the Central Asian plateau.

This disconnect is the source of Beijing’s persistent mismanagement of the Tibetan Plateau. From the catastrophic commune-era terracing of highland barley fields to the forced relocation of traditional nomads, Sino-centric policies that ignore Tibetan voices and fragile ecological realities have consistently proven disastrous. Yet, even amidst today’s global environmental crisis, Beijing demonstrates no intention of drawing upon centuries of Tibetan cultural wisdom, a heritage globally recognized for its deep commitment to human harmony, environmental ethics and peace.

While open societies increasingly turn to Indigenous knowledge to combat the modern ecological crisis, China, by contrast, is stepping up efforts to eradicate the “minority” cultures. Decades after the Indian residential school system in North America was dismantled and recognized globally as a tragic mistake, Beijing implemented that exact same system in Tibet to erase a rich and unique civilization, and proudly codified it into the country’s law this year.

If China continues to ignore the potential seismic and ecological consequences of its actions in the Himalayas, and continues to systematically dismantle the only culture equipped to manage the plateau’s fragile ecosystem, it accelerates the clock on destructive glacial lake outburst floods and pushes the Tibetan environment further out of balance. But what happens in Tibet doesn’t stay in Tibet. It eventually flows downstream into neighboring countries, including China itself. China’s dams may fail to hold the ten trillion cubic meters of surface water hanging 20,000 feet above the lowland plains.

Should any of the 95,000 dams China has built ever fail, the 1931 Yangtze River flood , which claimed 3 million lives in China, might no longer hold the record for history’s deadliest disaster in that country. But these dams don’t just threaten Chinese lives. People in Tibet, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam are in line for the same threat.

The 6th century Chinese poet named Yu Xin wisely wrote: “Those who eat the fruit think of the tree; those who drink the stream cherish its source.” Beijing’s leaders, instead of following the cultureless hardlining bloc who views Tibetan culture as a threat to China’s interest, might do better to reflect on their own ancestral wisdom. The very culture they are attempting to destroy may hold the key to securing China’s future in an era of catastrophic climate change.

Tenzin Bhagen (Yeshi Dorje) is a Tibetan writer, a former journalist for Voice of America and Radio Free Asia who had previously worked for environmental protection in the Himalayas.

articles.title: Tillis calls Trump Jr. wedding gift from Russian oligarch ‘stupid on stilts’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) chastised Donald Trump Jr. on Sunday for accepting a wedding gift from a Russian oligarch. “This was stupid on stilts … This is a man who’s worth somewhere between $300 million and $400 million,” Tillis said on CNN’s “State of the Union,” referring to Umar Kremlev. ProPublica reported earlier this month…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) chastised Donald Trump Jr. on Sunday for accepting a wedding gift from a Russian oligarch.

“This was stupid on stilts … This is a man who’s worth somewhere between $300 million and $400 million,” Tillis said on CNN’s “State of the Union,” referring to Umar Kremlev.

ProPublica reported earlier this month that Kremlev, who has ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, heavily funded and attended the Caribbean wedding of President Trump’s eldest son and Bettina Trump.

GOP Sen. John Curtis (Utah) asked the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday to subpoena Trump Jr. regarding the matter .

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) backed up Curtis later in the day, with Tillis also saying the panel should launch a probe after the midterms.

While the North Carolina Republican said Sunday he “would leave it to” Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) regarding the “mechanics” of getting the president’s son to testify, he deemed Kremlev’s wedding gift a “bad look.”

“This is amateur hour, at a time when we need our pros on the field. We have got an election we need to win in 37 days. How this helped, I can’t imagine,” he told host Jake Tapper.

“Maybe Don Jr. can give us a reasonable example for why tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars from an oligarch went into a wedding in some beach location,” Tillis later remarked. “But, boy, I’d sure like to see the rationale behind it.

“On its face, it doesn’t look very smart.”

The president said earlier this month that his son repaid Kremlev for the gift. Bettina Trump also defended the gift , writing on Instagram that Kremlev “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER” their wedding.

“Friendship doesn’t require a political motive,” she wrote on Sept. 14 . “Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.”

articles.title: Mark Kelly: Trump ‘stuck’ with Iran and wants to ‘get back to where he was before’ war started
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) on Sunday said President Trump is “stuck” with handling the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran and is seeking a path to “get back to where” the U.S. was before the war began in February. “The president got into this without a strategic goal, without a plan, without a timeline, without an exit…
articles.body:
Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) on Sunday said President Trump is “stuck” with handling the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran and is seeking a path to “get back to where” the U.S. was before the war began in February.

“The president got into this without a strategic goal, without a plan, without a timeline, without an exit strategy. He’s stuck,” Kelly told host Martha Raddatz on ABC News’s “This Week.”

Kelly called for “professionals” to handle negotiations with Iran instead of the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, adding that the U.S. cannot leave Iran with the “strength” to develop nuclear weapons. The Trump administration has said preventing Iran from developing and obtaining nuclear weapons has been its primary objective with the military campaign.

“I think what the president would love to do is get back to where he was before he started this thing,” the Arizona Democrat said. “The Iranians weren’t racing to get a nuclear weapon. The straits were open, and we didn’t have over 20 dead service members and 800 injured. This thing has been a disaster, and it’s been a mistake and it’s because of the failed leadership of the president.”

Raddatz asked about the damage to buildings in U.S. bases in several Gulf countries, which Kelly said was “significant.” Combined with other expenses going toward the military campaign, the senator said the total cost of the war could be an “excess of $40 billion at this point with no end in sight because the president doesn’t know what to do.”

An American Enterprise Institute report released in April showed that about 70 structures at 11 U.S. military bases in the Middle East have sustained $5 billion in damage. The damage has stirred some debate about the future of the U.S. military presence in the Middle East.

Trump on Saturday publicly rejected Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter a ceasefire. He accused the regime of “losing so badly” and that the U.S. has “total control of the Hormuz Strait” with “massive amounts of oil” departing the vital waterway.

Roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported out of the strait. Iran effectively shut it down following the outbreak of the conflict, blasting gas prices to new records. The national average for gas in the U.S. hit $4.48 on Sunday, with last year’s average down at $3.14, according to AAA.

Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, disputed Trump’s rejection of the peace proposal to NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” on Sunday.

“If they reject it with no reason, this is their fault,” Araghchi said of U.S. negotiators. “And I have to say that although we heard from President Trump that he’s rejecting this deal, we are still waiting for an official response through the mediators.”

articles.title: Sen. John Fetterman says it's "entirely possible" Democrats take back Senate
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said that it's "entirely possible" his party wins control of the Senate in the midterm elections, while leavin...
articles.body:
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said Saturday that it's "entirely possible" his party could win control of the Senate in the midterm elections, but he also left the door open on his own political future.

"Let's revisit after the midterm," Fetterman told CBS News' Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin .

Democrats faced an uphill battle heading into the midterm cycle as they sought control the upper chamber, with 53 Republicans currently in the Senate and a map that appeared more favorable to the GOP. But as affordability issues have persisted in the Trump administration and amid the unpopular war with Iran, the picture has appeared to improve for Democrats as they aim to secure a majority in the Senate.

Fetterman, who delivered Democrats a crucial victory in a closely watched race in 2022, has been under scrutiny in recent years for breaking with his party, spurring questions about his future. Asked whether he would leave the Democratic Party, Fetterman said Saturday that he doesn't "have a reason to." And he emphasized, "I am not a Republican." But he cautioned that people should wait until the midterm elections to "see what I do."

"Let's see what happens if I happen to be 51 — I don't know," Fetterman said.

Fetterman shocked many Democrats when he made a video appearance at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month introducing his counterpart, GOP Sen. Dave McCormick, while vowing to work with President Trump on steel.

But Fetterman said Saturday, "I have no path as a Republican."

The Pennsylvania Democrat said, "There are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party."

"How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterm and see what happens," he said. "And now, if we do win and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania."

Pennsylvania is one of only two states in the country represented by one Democrat and one Republican in the Senate, alongside Wisconsin. A third state, Maine, has one Republican senator and one independent who caucuses with Democrat. Pennsylvania has flipped between supporting Democrats and Republican presidents in recent elections.

On whether he'll seek reelection in 2028 , Fetterman said he's been actively fundraising, but he also indicated that the decision will come after the midterms.

Fetterman posed the question, "Where's the Democratic Party at right now?" He pointed to attendance at a nearby event with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and "the energy" among the party, which has seen a series of wins by insurgent Democrats in recent months. He cited his commitment to Israel as an issue underscoring his divergence from some of the party, adding, "more and more members of my caucus are becoming more and more anti-Israel."

He also pointed to the recent government shutdowns as an issue he diverged from the bulk of Democrats on, arguing that he's "putting the country over the party" and fighting for workers.

"Do you think it's right and smart to shut our government down? No, Democrats, we used to say, 'No, never, never do that,'" Fetterman said. "And that put me at the odds of my caucus, saying, 'It's wrong.'"

Fetterman said he's "chosen to be country over the party, knowing that some of these decisions are going to put me at odds."

Asked whether he expects Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to remain leader if Democrats take the majority, and whether he would vote for him, Fetterman said, "Yes, I mean, there's no one making a move."

Fetterman called a Marist poll that shows Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek up eight points in Iowa "shocking," among other races where Democrats are leading in some polls. He pointed to Schumer's recruiting efforts, saying, "If people are angry at Chuck Schumer, it's undeniable, he has recruited an incredibly strong class."

"I don't sharpen blades for Chuck Schumer, and there might be some people there that refuse to say it, but it's not helpful to go after our leader because we have no idea until we wait until the midterm," Fetterman said. "It's irrelevant until what happens in the midterm."

articles.title: Kennedy suggests ‘rule’ that no politician should have a building named after them while alive
articles.summary: GOP Sen. John Kennedy (La.) said Sunday that public officials should not have buildings named after them while they are alive, as President Trump fights to rename the Kennedy Center after himself. During an interview on CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” Kennedy said public officials, including Trump, should not “spend public money on private ads…
articles.body:
GOP Sen. John Kennedy (La.) said Sunday that public officials should not have buildings named after them while they are alive, as President Trump fights to rename the Kennedy Center after himself.

During an interview on CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” Kennedy said public officials, including Trump, should not “spend public money on private ads for themselves.”

The Louisiana Republican made his remarks as a new ad promoting Trump — which was funded with taxpayer money — appears on multiple networks.

“The White House sees it differently, but … you can’t spend public money to … promote yourself,” Kennedy told host Margaret Brennan.

The Republican senator then took it a step further, saying it should be illegal for public officials to have a building named after them while they are alive.

“I may end up with a sombrero on my head, but I also think we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him when he’s alive,” he quipped, referring to the president mocking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries last year by sharing doctored videos of them donning sombreros .

Throughout his second term, Trump has attempted to rename multiple buildings after himself. That includes the Kennedy Center, but a federal judge invalidated multiple attempts from the Trump-aligned board to add the president’s name to the facility.

The State Department also added Trump’s name to the U.S. Institute of Peace last December. But former institute employees, whom the administration ousted, filed a court motion earlier this month to stop construction crews from carving the president’s name onto the exterior of the building.

“The threatened carving would impose serious irreparable harm,” the attorneys for the former employees wrote in their emergency filing . “It is a discrete act that can and should be forestalled through a limited, status-quo-preserving modification of the stay pending appeal.”

articles.title: Blanche claims Trump ‘hasn’t denied access’ to White House reporters
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday claimed that President Trump did not deny White House reporters access to the executive mansion, after the president banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from the grounds and had their passes confiscated by Secret Service. “Well, the president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told host Martha Raddatz during the…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday claimed that President Trump did not deny White House reporters access to the executive mansion, after the president banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from the grounds and had their passes confiscated by Secret Service.

“Well, the president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told host Martha Raddatz during the attorney general’s Sunday appearance on ABC News’s “This Week.”

“That’s not the right way to describe it. This is what the president has said –– is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news.”

Blanche emphasized that reporters’ access to the White House is a privilege but said Trump made his decision “after years and years of one-sided media coverage” that was “not fair to the American people.”

A federal judge on Thursday sided with the three media outlets to immediately restore their press credentials. The outlets had filed a lawsuit against the administration. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump nominee, ruled that the ban likely violated the reporters’ constitutional due process rights.

The attorney general said Trump had “every right” to bar CNN’s reporters from joining the White House press pool on Air Force One despite the ruling. He added that reporting that is “complete misinformation” rises to a “national security problem” for U.S. relations with other countries.

“What I’m talking about is the government’s position, and that’s what the Department of Justice said in court, which is the same thing that President Trump has said repeatedly, which is at some point, the complete misinformation and the inaccuracy on the one-sided news out of certain organizations does become a national security issue,” Blanche said.

Raddatz asked if this means reporters would be screened before joining the press pool on Air Force One, to which Blanche said no. Reporting on the president “doesn’t have to be good” or all positive, he later said before accusing the coverage of the president as an attempt to “diminish the Republicans and the Republican administration.”

The president initially said he banned the three outlets over their reporting before later saying last Monday that it had to do with national security .

“Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social that day.

The focus on national security has been a blanket rationale for other legal tests against the administration’s proposals, including construction on the White House ballroom and the proposed triumphal arch . The Justice Department used this argument before Kelly, adding that coverage of the White House is a “privilege” and that Trump has the ability to “consider journalists’ viewpoints” when granting that access.
