articles.title: If Trump is serious about antisemitism, he should reopen this lifeline for refugees
articles.summary: As Congress faces a Sept. 30 deadline to reauthorize the Lautenberg Amendment, critics argue the Trump administration has undermined the program by closing the processing centers essential for helping Iranian religious minorities escape persecution.
articles.body:
Congress faces a Sept. 30 deadline to reauthorize the Lautenberg Amendment , a refugee program that has, for decades, helped Jews escape antisemitism in Iran. But the Trump administration has effectively shut the program down, by closing the processing centers that allow it to work. An odd choice for an administration that rarely misses a chance to tell us how seriously it takes antisemitism .

The Lautenberg-Specter program was enacted in 1990 to help persecuted Jews and Christians in the Soviet Union reunite with family in the United States, then expanded in 2004 to include religious minorities in Iran. Congress has reauthorized it on a bipartisan basis ever since. The danger it was meant to answer has not gone away and, indeed, may have only become more inflamed. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) has called Iran “the worst source of antisemitism in the world.” The bipartisan U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom says Iran is sponsoring “a global campaign of antisemitism,” targeting Jews and Jewish sites. And yet the Trump administration has closed one of the few paths built specifically to help them, and others persecuted because of their faith, escape.

The Lautenberg-Specter program has hardly been an open door. For Iranian religious minorities, the way out began with someone already in the United States, a family member or friend willing to sponsor them and help support them once they arrived. Jews, Christians, Baha’is, Zoroastrians, and Sabean Mandaeans began their applications in Iran and, because the United States has no embassy there to interview them, those who reached the next stage left Iran for Austria.

There, the Resettlement Support Center in Vienna received their applications, prepared the documents, arranged interviews with U.S. government officials and mandatory medical examinations, and helped with the paperwork for their eventual placement in the United States, while American law enforcement carried out background and security checks.

More than 33,000 members of Iran’s religious minorities made it through that system between 2001 and 2025. When the State Department ended the grant that paid for the center, which the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society had run in partnership with the government for over 25 years, more than 14,000 Iranians were still in the pipeline. The society no longer knows what has happened to many of them. The organization lost access to the government data it used to follow individual cases when the processing center closed. Its public guidance now directs applicants seeking information about their cases to the State Department or their representatives in Congress.

The people waiting in the Lautenberg pipeline have had more reason to leave in the past year than ever before. Since the war with Israel began, Iranian authorities arrested more than 20,000 people , including members of the country’s Baha’i, Christian and Jewish minorities. Baha’is were arrested, interrogated and had their homes raided and property confiscated; even before the war, authorities in Urmia had sealed four Baha’i-owned businesses after their owners closed them to observe a religious holiday.

At least 35 Jews in Tehran and Shiraz were summoned and interrogated about relatives in Israel, and members of the Jewish community were arrested in three provinces, some facing accusations of espionage. At least 54 Christians were reportedly arrested in the month after the war. The campaign has reached beyond Iran as well. In January 2025, an officer in Iran’s Quds Force recruited a Georgian drug trafficker and offered him $200,000 to assassinate Rabbi Shneor Segal in Azerbaijan, a plot Azerbaijani authorities broke up before it could be carried out. Trump’s restrictions on travel from Iran even include an explicit exception for immigrant visas for “ethnic and religious minorities facing persecution in Iran.”

Trump has made antisemitism one of the causes of his second presidency. He has created a federal task force to combat it, ordered agencies to use the government’s legal powers against it, and promised to confront it “at home and abroad.” His administration has investigated universities , threatened billions of dollars in federal funding , and pursued foreign students over what it says is “violent anti-Semitic incidents on campus.”

Yet in Iran, where Jews have been interrogated about relatives in Israel, arrested on suspicion of espionage, and surveilled in their own synagogues, one of the oldest American programs for getting them out has been dismantled.

By the end of this month, Congress should reauthorize Lautenberg. The administration should refund and reopen the processing centers that support it. Fourteen thousand stranded people, and their families in America, are waiting to see whether Trump’s promises about fighting antisemitism abroad mean anything when Jews facing persecution actually need a way out.

Mia Emmunah Toubian is an Iranian American journalist and human-rights researcher whose work at Harvard Medical School investigated the treatment of women political prisoners in Iran. Jason Bryan Silverstein is a writer and anthropologist focused on health and human rights, and he directs the Media, Medicine, and Health Program at Harvard Medical School.

articles.title: Beshear: More states within ‘margin of error’ for Democratic gubernatorial candidates
articles.summary: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) said Sunday the party is looking to pick up multiple GOP-controlled governor’s mansions in November. “If we went back a year ago, Democrats were trying to pick themselves off the floor,” Beshear told host Jake Tapper on CNN’s “State of the Union.” But the chair of the Democratic Governors Association…
articles.body:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) said Sunday the party is looking to pick up multiple GOP-controlled governor’s mansions in November.

“If we went back a year ago, Democrats were trying to pick themselves off the floor,” Beshear told host Jake Tapper on CNN’s “ State of the Union .”

But the chair of the Democratic Governors Association argued that New Jersey Gov. Mike Sherrill (D) and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) winning their races last year gave Democrats “some winds behind our sails.”

Beshear told host Jake Tapper, “Now, because Donald Trump’s agenda is hurting our American families so badly, we have even more states that are suddenly in the margin of error, Florida, Texas, Alaska, Nebraska. The map’s getting really big.”

Election handicapper Cook Political Report has shifted multiple governor’s races to the left in recent months.

That includes Florida , where former GOP Rep. David Jolly (Fla.), a converted Democrat, is taking on Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.). As of Friday, Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s polling partner, gave Donalds a 67 percent chance to win, up 8 points from the day prior.

Another race Beshear mentioned was the Texas gubernatorial battle between state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) and Gov. Greg Abbott (R). Recent polling forecasts a competitive race , although DDHQ still gave the incumbent a roughly 7 in 10 chance of securing a record fourth term.

“We’re talking every day with that campaign, and it’s just so exciting to see [Hinojosa] and James Talarico, me being a Southern Democrat, making a Southern state competitive again,” Beshear said Sunday, referring to Talarico’s Senate race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

DDHQ also gives Democrats a 51 percent chance of flipping the House and Senate, which would give the party control of Congress for the final two years of President Trump’s term. If that occurs, Beshear said the party has to be “for something” and not just against Trump.

“Far too many people believe and feel the economy is rigged, it’s not working for them,” he told Tapper.

Beshear later said, “There is an opportunity here. But to take advantage of it, Democrats need to not just win in November. We’re going to have to govern well.”

articles.title: El Ayuntamiento de Madrid exige a la Delegación del Gobierno que "reponga cuanto antes" la normalidad en Sol
articles.standfirst: El Consistorio acusa a la Delegación y al Ministerio del Interior de "dejación de funciones" por permitir la acampada tras la manifestación por el derecho a la vivienda
articles.summary: El Consistorio acusa a la Delegación y al Ministerio del Interior de "dejación de funciones" por permitir la acampada tras la manifestación por el derecho a la vivienda
articles.body: El Ayuntamiento de Madrid ha exigido este domingo a la Delegación del Gobierno que actúe para "reponer cuanto antes" la normalidad en la Puerta del Sol, donde cientos de personas permanecen acampadas desde la noche del sábado tras la manifestación convocada para reclamar medidas frente a la crisis de la vivienda. El Consistorio ha mostrado su "sorpresa" e "indignación" ante la continuidad de la protesta y ha responsabilizado directamente a la Delegación del Gobierno en Madrid de la situación. En un comunicado, el Ayuntamiento sostiene que la acampada es consecuencia de una supuesta "dejación de funciones" y de la falta de diligencia de la Delegación y del Ministerio del Interior. La protesta comenzó después de la manifestación celebrada el sábado en Madrid contra el desahucio de Maricarmen y para reclamar medidas urgentes en materia de vivienda. Después de la marcha, parte de los participantes regresó a la Puerta del Sol y comenzó a instalar tiendas de campaña, dando lugar a la acampada que continúa este domingo. El Gobierno de José Luis Martínez-Almeida cuestiona también la actuación de las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad durante la protesta. Según el Consistorio, cuando comenzaron los asentamientos, la Policía Nacional se retiró de sus emplazamientos, por lo que reclama a la Delegación del Gobierno y al Ministerio del Interior que expliquen si esa retirada respondió a una orden directa del delegado. El Ayuntamiento ha calificado la acampada de "ilegal" y considera que lo ocurrido es consecuencia de una "falta de diligencia" por parte de la Delegación del Gobierno y del Ministerio del Interior. El Consistorio plantea incluso que se aclare si la permanencia de los manifestantes en Sol fue fruto de una decisión deliberada. "La Delegación del Gobierno no puede mirar para otro lado ni cargar a otra administración con los problemas que causa su incapacidad e incompetencia para realizar sus funciones", ha señalado el Ayuntamiento, que exige que se aborden las consecuencias de la acampada y se reponga la normalidad en la Puerta del Sol cuanto antes. En su comunicado, el Ayuntamiento de Madrid recuerda además el precedente de las movilizaciones del 15M de 2011, cuando la Puerta del Sol también se convirtió en el epicentro de una acampada. Según el Consistorio, en aquella ocasión los desalojos fueron organizados y coordinados por la Delegación del Gobierno. Por ello, el Gobierno municipal reclama ahora una explicación sobre la actuación de la Delegación y sobre la retirada de los agentes de la Policía Nacional cuando comenzaron los asentamientos. La protesta se mantiene vinculada a las reivindicaciones del movimiento por la vivienda, cuyos participantes reclaman al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez medidas frente a los problemas de acceso a la vivienda y, en particular, la aprobación del denominado 'decreto Maricarmen'.
